a_rows_sample.statement: Structural (by-construction) explanation for why congruence held in every test: T's derived signature K x Op x Policy x Authority -harpoon-> K x Outcome does not include History in its domain, so T cannot depend on it — a function cannot depend on an argument it does not receive. This holds under exactly two assumptions: A1 (T reads only K, Policy, Authority — PROVEN by elimination of actor/time/evidence/context during signature derivation) and A2 (no operation consults order-of-arrival — HOLDS for the twelve derived operations because A and R are sets, making order structurally unobservable).

a_rows_sample.anchor: A2 is the one that could fail. Any future operation reading insertion order — "the first assertion wins", "the most recently added is authoritative" — breaks congruence immediately. That is a design constraint the theory now states explicitly rather than assumes silently.
a_rows_sample.statement: Explicit forward-looking design constraint: assumption A2 (no operation consults insertion order) is violable by future design — any future operation implementing 'first assertion wins' or 'most recently added is authoritative' semantics would break congruence immediately; the theory now states this as an explicit constraint rather than a silent assumption.

a_rows_sample.anchor: SUFFICIENT UNDER ASSUMPTIONS. Not sufficient unqualified: the assumptions are real and A2 is violable by future design. Not insufficient: no counterexample exists and none can, given A1. Not unknown: the test was constructed correctly and executed.
a_rows_sample.statement: Final classification: the Knowledge-State/History sufficiency question is SUFFICIENT UNDER ASSUMPTIONS — deliberately neither 'sufficient unqualified' (the assumptions A1/A2 are real and A2 is violable), nor 'insufficient' (no counterexample exists, and none can given A1), nor 'unknown' (the test was validly constructed and executed).

a_rows_sample.anchor: Knowledge State is sufficient for FUTURE COMPUTATION. It is NOT sufficient for GOVERNANCE AUDIT. ... Who asserted this, and when? NO ... Was every admission properly authorised? NO — GovernanceValid(K,Γ) needs History ... What did we believe last March? NO — needs History
a_rows_sample.statement: The state/history sufficiency boundary is drawn precisely: K alone answers what is currently held, what follows from an operation (congruence), whether structural/semantic invariants hold, and current epistemic status (recomputable from e); K alone CANNOT answer who asserted something and when, whether every admission was properly authorised (GovernanceValid(K,Gamma) needs History), or what was believed at a past point in time (needs History or a bitemporal interpretation of t).

a_rows_sample.anchor: K answers what is known. History answers how it came to be known and by whom. Neither reduces to the other, and T needs only the first.
a_rows_sample.statement: Governing principle stated as the resolution of the state/history boundary the programme has circled since the executed History(K)!=K counterexample: K answers what is known; History answers how it came to be known and by whom; neither reduces to the other, and the transformation function T needs only K.

a_rows_sample.anchor: The decisive discrimination: a policy is an OBJECT that is applied, not a function that is called. It has identity, a version, an applicability window, and it can be composed and compared. A bare function has none of those. ... versioning is only meaningful for an object.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Policy = (id, version, Gates, ValidityInterval, ResolutionBehavior) ... Gates : SET of three-valued predicates g : Decision → {True, False, Unknown} ... ValidityInterval : [vf, vt) ... ResolutionBehavior : Unknown → Block | Allow ... Apply(p,d) = False if ∃g∈p.Gates: g(d)=False ← strict conjunction,
a_rows_sample.statement: The derived canonical Policy type: Policy=(id, version, Gates, ValidityInterval, ResolutionBehavior), where Gates is a set of three-valued predicates over a Decision, ValidityInterval is a half-open temporal window, and ResolutionBehavior maps Unknown to Block or Allow; the Apply function is a strict three-valued conjunction over Gates (False if any gate is False, ResolutionBehavior(Unknown) if any gate is Unknown and none is False, True otherwise, with no averaging), and Applicable(p,t) checks temporal membership in the validity interval — this directly answers gap G-2.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Gates is a SET, not a tuple — PROVEN, not chosen. Executed: two policies differing only in gate order are structurally unequal but extensionally equal. Order is representation; a tuple leaks it into identity.
a_rows_sample.statement: Executed proof that Gates must be a set rather than an ordered tuple: two policies differing only in gate order are found structurally unequal but extensionally (behaviorally) equal — a tuple representation would leak arbitrary insertion order into policy identity, which is wrong; this is PROVEN by the order-difference test, not a stylistic choice.

a_rows_sample.anchor: codomain {True, False, Unknown} — three-valued ... totality partial — undefined outside ValidityInterval ... composability ∧ only — meet-semilattice; ∨ REFUTED ... identity (id, version); version is semantically load-bearing ... executed: same id, different ResolutionBehavior, different result ... p
a_rows_sample.statement: Per-property analysis of Policy: three-valued codomain, partial totality (undefined outside its validity interval), deterministic given fixed gates, composable only under conjunction (a meet-semilattice; disjunction is REFUTED as a composition operator), four distinct equality notions (deferred to a companion artifact 5), identity is (id,version) with version proven semantically load-bearing (same id with different ResolutionBehavior gives a different Apply result), versioning required (corpus names v3 policies), and policy provenance (who authored/authorised it) explicitly recorded as absent from the governing corpus definition (step 57.47) — an unresolved gap.

a_rows_sample.statement: The corpus's independently-stated 'no averaging' rule for policy gates (a 95%-admissible decision, i.e. 3 of 4 gates true, is still inadmissible if even one is false) is confirmed by an independent measurement-theoretic argument: gates are nominal/boolean and JustificationStrength is ordinal, and neither scale admits arithmetic — averaging four booleans would require an interval scale that does not exist for either; the corpus's rule and the verifier's own scale-theory constraint are shown to be the identical constraint, derived twice via two independent routes.

a_rows_sample.statement: Experiment 3, run against the real 37-document EKP, FAILS to demonstrate policy-dependence (lenient and strict policies produce identical True/False:24/13 splits, 0 differing documents); an initial false claim ('SAME K, DIFFERENT POLICY, DIFFERENT ASSESSMENT') is explicitly retained rather than deleted, and diagnosed: the differing gate (JustifStrength) never fails independently of Authorization because, empirically, every document with authoritative/derived authority also has an approved-class status — status and authority are declared independent in authorities.yaml but are almost perfectly collinear in the EKP's actual current content, showing orthogonality is a design property, not an observed data property; the methodological consequence is that policy-comparison experiments prove nothing on non-discriminating datasets, and this one would have passed silently if the numbers had not been checked against the prose claim.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Policy ≠ Knowledge State ... K was byte-identical in both runs; only the policy varied ... PROVEN | Policy ≠ Evidence ... the evidence is unchanged while P_A admits and P_B refuses ... PROVEN | Policy ≠ Assertion Status (Σ) ... Σ is the output of Assessment(·, Policy) ... refutes step 199 ... PROVEN
a_rows_sample.statement: Seven placements of Policy are each PROVEN false with a specific executed counterexample: (1) Policy != Knowledge State, since the same K (37 real EKP assertions) evaluated under two policies stayed byte-identical while only the policy varied; (2) Policy != Evidence, since a fixed piece of evidence (nsrc=1, origin=blog) is admitted by one policy and refused by another, so evidence cannot both be and judge itself; (3) Policy != Assertion Status Sigma, since Sigma is the OUTPUT of Assessment(.,Policy), directly refuting step 199's 'Policy = Allowed' conflation (Allowed is Apply(p,d)'s codomain, not p); (4) Policy != Validation Result, since Apply(P_B,D2)=False's result dict is a value produced by the reusable policy object, not the object itself; (5) Policy != Governance Status Gamma, since 37 real assertions carry 5 distinct Gamma values under a single policy (Gamma is a property of an assertion, Policy a property of the regime); (6) Policy != Assessment, since Assessment:P x Evidence x Context x Policy -> Sigma takes Policy as an argument, and a function cannot be its own parameter (this is why the Policy:Claim x Evidence x Context->Assessment candidate was rejected in artifact 2); (7) Policy != Transformation History, since Policy is an input to T while History is an output of it, and two histories reaching the same K can have been produced under different policies.

a_rows_sample.anchor: LocalCorrectness ⇏ GlobalCorrectness; compositional correctness via interface contracts
a_rows_sample.statement: States that each component C_i satisfying Correct(C_i) does not imply Correct(C_1∘...∘C_n): interactions can introduce failures absent from individual components (LocalCorrectness ⇏ GlobalCorrectness). Worked example: EvidenceContext and DecisionContext both correct, but a wrong translation between them makes Evidence->Decision incorrect despite both bounded contexts being internally correct -- 'exactly why context boundaries and contracts matter'. Formalizes compositional correctness: Correct(C1) ∧ Correct(C2) ∧ Contract(C1,C2) ⇒ Correct(C1∘C2), so the interface contract becomes part of the proof. Represents KOS conceptually as C_identity∘C_semantic∘C_evidence∘C_epistemic∘C_causal∘C_decision∘C_governance∘C_learning (conceptual composition, not one runtime pipeline).

a_rows_sample.anchor: Bounded contexts as proof boundaries; anti-corruption layer as semantic-preserving translation
a_rows_sample.statement: If BC_i guarantees I_i and its interface guarantees Contract_i, another context can rely on Contract_i -- 'this enables compositional reasoning'. Concludes bounded contexts are not merely organizational boxes but Proof boundaries, each owning semantics, invariants, state transitions, and contracts. Formalizes an anti-corruption layer's translation Model_A -> Model_B via Preserve(T,I) (translation T preserves invariant I); example: if Approved in Context A has richer meaning than Approved in Context B, a direct field mapping is invalid and the translation must explicitly encode a SemanticMapping. A ContractViolation must become an explicit state/event, never disappearing silently -- giving the property: invalid input must not silently become valid knowledge.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Twelve falsification experiments for Step 48 global-invariant/correctness model (all PASS)
a_rows_sample.statement: Runs twelve falsification tests, all PASS: (1) a component is locally correct but its interface translation violates semantics => global invariant failure detected; (2) all safety properties hold but a workflow deadlocks => safety passes, liveness fails; (3) evidence is modified without a new version => evidence-integrity violation; (4) a decision uses a model created after the decision date => temporal/historical-integrity violation; (5) an AI proposal bypasses authorization => AI-boundary and authorization invariants fail; (6) a causal claim has no documented assumptions => causal-integrity violation; (7) a trusted claim becomes invalid but remains operational without review => revision/invalidation-invariant violation; (8) a safety-critical unknown is treated as true => unknown-state/safety-invariant violation; (9) a claim valid in one bounded context is applied to another without semantic mapping => scope/semantic-integrity violation; (10) two distributed replicas temporarily disagree where eventual consistency is permitted => no violation if the declared consistency contract allows it; (11) two replicas disagree on a strong-consistency invariant => critical consistency violation; (12) a model is stable and highly confident but external validation shows systematic error => epistemic correctness fails despite model stability.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Cross-context invariants resolved via contracts (Query/Result), never by merging aggregates
a_rows_sample.statement: Example cross-context invariant Execute(Action) ⇒ Authorized(Decision) spans DecisionContext and GovernanceContext; these must not be forced into one aggregate. Instead contexts communicate through a Contract: DecisionContext -> AuthorizationQuery, receiving AuthorizationResult -- this preserves ownership (Governance owns Authorization, Decision owns Decision; neither steals the other's model). Depicts a logical context-map flow Evidence -> Knowledge -> {Causal, and Semantic feeding Decision} -> Decision -> Governance -> Action -> Outcome -> Learning -> back to Knowledge, explicitly 'a logical flow, not necessarily synchronous runtime communication'. Anti-corruption layers ACL_AB translate Model_A -> Model_B preserving the semantic contract; example: Evidence Context's Observation(source,timestamp,value) maps to Knowledge Context's Evidence(proposition,scope,relevance) via SemanticTransformation, not FieldToField mapping.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Formal context composition B_i=(M_i,Γ_i,I_i); Preserve(T_ij,I_required); LocalInvariant+ContractInvariant⇒GlobalInvariant links back to Step 48
a_rows_sample.statement: Defines a context as B_i=(M_i,Gamma_i,I_i) (internal model, published contracts, invariants), a context interaction T_ij: Gamma_i -> M_j required to preserve semantics (Preserve(T_ij,I_required)), and the complete system as KOS = direct-sum_i B_i with explicit contracts Gamma_ij, with the goal LocalInvariant + ContractInvariant ⇒ GlobalInvariant -- explicitly connecting Step 53 back to Step 48's compositional correctness result. Declares STEP 53 -- PASS and states the important result is not merely that communication works but that 'KnowledgeOS boundaries are semantic and contractual, not merely technical'. Opens Step 54 (Mathematical Types -> DDD Domain Types -> Executable Contracts): deriving an actual type system from P={Entity,State,Event,Observation,Proposition,Relation,Policy,Action} down to concrete types (EntityId, Observation, Evidence, Claim, Relation, KnowledgeSnapshot, Policy, Decision, Authorization, Action, Outcome) each with explicit Invariant, Ownership, Lifecycle, Version, Provenance, Contract -- 'the point at which our mathematical architecture can begin to translate directly into the actual KnowledgeOS software design'.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Compositionality hypothesis: I_A ∧ I_B ∧ Contract_AB ⇒ I_AB; CorrectContexts ⇏ CorrectComposition
a_rows_sample.statement: For B_A=(M_A,Gamma_A,I_A) and B_B=(M_B,Gamma_B,I_B) both individually satisfying their invariants, tests whether I_A ∧ I_B ∧ Contract_AB is sufficient for I_AB (LocalCorrectness + CorrectContract ⇒ GlobalCorrectness). Worked example Evidence->Knowledge: I_E (Evidence(E) ⇒ Integrity(E)) and I_K (ValidatedClaim(C) ⇒ Provenance(C)) can each hold while an incorrect EvidenceId_A->ClaimId_B mapping still breaks the global system, giving CorrectContexts ⇏ CorrectComposition -- contract correctness is needed too, requiring an explicit integration invariant I_EK (Claim(C) derived from E ⇒ E is an admissible evidence reference).

a_rows_sample.anchor: Identifiers crossing boundaries need semantic integrity; content-addressable Hash(E) verification against tampering
a_rows_sample.statement: Experiment: valid evidence mapping E1->ACL_EK->C1 with Provenance(C1)=E1 verified -- PASS. Experiment: a deliberately wrong mapping (E1 published but mapped to E2) is detected provided the contract includes identity/integrity verification -- PASS, revealing that identifiers crossing boundaries need semantic integrity. Strengthens external references with content-addressable verification: Reference=(EvidenceId,Version,Hash), consumer checks Hash_received=Hash_expected; a tampered E1 (hash h'!=h) is detected as IntegrityFailure and must not be silently accepted -- PASS.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Mutable-live-reference hazard discovered and corrected: DecisionBasis must be immutable/version-bound (KnowledgeSnapshotRef)
a_rows_sample.statement: Composition Knowledge->Decision requires the global invariant Basis(D)=K_t for the snapshot used to construct D; experiment with a fixed immutable snapshot reference PASSes, but a deliberately mutable live reference to CurrentKnowledge (K1->K2 mutating what D1 sees) produces FAILURE DETECTED -- 'a useful failure... the mathematical architecture itself survives, but a naive implementation would violate it'. Architectural correction: strengthen the contract to KnowledgeSnapshotRef=(SnapshotId,Version,Hash), so a decision stores the reference, never a mutable live knowledge object -- giving the rule DecisionBasis must be immutable or version-bound.

a_rows_sample.anchor: PolicyAtDecision != CurrentPolicy; historical vs current authorization query distinction
a_rows_sample.statement: Composition Decision->Governance requires Authorization(D,P) ⇒ DecisionBasis and PolicyVersion are identifiable. Experiment: D1 created under P1, policy replaced by P2 -- authorization must not silently re-evaluate historical D1 under P2, PASS provided authorization semantics distinguish PolicyAtDecision from CurrentPolicy. Distinguishes two legitimate but different questions: the historical question ('was this decision valid under P1?') versus the current question ('would this decision be authorized under today's policy?') -- Authorize_historical(D,t) != Authorize_current(D).

a_rows_sample.anchor: Authorization TOCTOU race discovered and corrected: Execute(A,t)⇒AuthorizationValid(A,t) with an explicit validity-window contract
a_rows_sample.statement: Composition Governance->Action requires Execute(A) ⇒ ValidAuthorization(A), raising a classic time-of-check/time-of-use problem: authorization checked True at t1, expired by t2, execution at t3 blindly relying on the earlier check violates the global invariant -- FAILURE DETECTED (again 'valuable'). Architectural correction: an Authorization type = (DecisionId, PolicyVersion, Authority, IssuedAt, ExpiresAt, AuthorizationId), execution must verify t_execute in [IssuedAt,ExpiresAt] (potentially revalidating immediately before execution), giving the strengthened invariant Execute(A,t) ⇒ AuthorizationValid(A,t), not merely AuthorizationValid(A,t_check).

a_rows_sample.anchor: Correlation contract needs both WID and ActionId; Learning bypass rejected; multi-agent proposal preservation and optimistic-concurrency conflict
a_rows_sample.statement: Composition Action->Outcome: a deliberate outcome-mixup (O1 associated to A2 instead of A1) is detected if action identity and correlation are validated -- PASS, showing a workflow CorrelationId=WID alone is too coarse and the specific ActionId is also needed. Composition Learning->Knowledge: Learning attempting UpdateClaim(C) directly is Rejected -- PASS, requiring Learning -> Proposal -> Validation -> KnowledgeRevision, never Learning -> DirectMutation. Composition multi-agent: Agent_A and Agent_B both proposing decisions P_A, P_B -- both preserved until a domain process determines the result -- PASS; concurrent modification of the same Decision(D) by both agents is controlled via Version/ConcurrencyToken, e.g. Version(D)=7 read by both, Agent A commits 7->8, Agent B's submission based on 7 yields ConcurrencyConflict -- PASS.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Global epistemic rule: absence of observed information != evidence of absence; closed-world vs open-world must be explicit per context/query
a_rows_sample.statement: Composition eventual consistency: EvidenceRegistered occurred but not yet visible to Knowledge Context; a concurrent Decision query must distinguish NotYetAvailable from DoesNotExist -- PASS, generalized to the global invariant: absence of observed information != evidence of absence, unless the domain explicitly defines closed-world semantics. Distinguishes closed-world (NotFound ⇒ False) from open-world (NotFound ⇒ Unknown) and requires KnowledgeOS to specify which applies per context/query.

a_rows_sample.anchor: No context may infer stronger semantics than its published contract justifies; TemporalOrder ⇏ Causality crosses contexts
a_rows_sample.statement: Composition semantic translation: a naive translator mapping Verified (Evidence Context) to Authorized (Decision Context) is invalid and rejected by the ACL absent an explicit semantic rule -- PASS, giving the global semantic invariant that no context may infer stronger semantics than the published contract justifies, 'one of the most important KnowledgeOS properties'. Composition Evidence->Causal: A precedes B does not automatically produce Causes(A,B) without an explicit causal basis -- PASS, restating TemporalOrder ⇏ Causality as a cross-context invariant.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Circular cross-context dependency detected via a Dependency Graph; feedback loop != deadlock; well-founded progress measure for productive cycles
a_rows_sample.statement: Constructs a circular context dependency (Decision needs Knowledge needs Evidence needs ExternalSource needs Authorization needs Decision) that is globally impossible despite every local rule being correct; detected as a Cycle -- PASS provided dependency analysis runs before workflow activation, revealing the need for an architecture-level Dependency Graph G_D=(Contexts,Dependencies), where cycles are not automatically invalid but workflow-critical cycles must be explicitly justified. Distinguishes FeedbackLoop != Deadlock: an intentional Learning<->Knowledge or Knowledge->Action->Outcome->Learning->Knowledge cycle is acceptable if there is temporal progression (Version_next>Version_current), whereas a nonproductive cycle (K_t->K_t->K_t with no progression) repeated indefinitely is a Liveness Failure. Introduces a well-founded progress measure mu(X) in W (no infinite descending chain, e.g. RemainingSteps in N) with each transition satisfying mu(X_{t+1})<mu(X_t), proving termination for a given workflow; distinguishes FiniteWorkflow from PersistentProcess (learning may continue indefinitely and needs Progress rather than termination, measured e.g. by new evidence, reduced uncertainty, improved model performance, validated knowledge, resolved conflicts).

a_rows_sample.anchor: Global eventual-consistency property under distributed execution; IntegrationState health concept; compositional observability (BlockedBecause)
a_rows_sample.statement: For separate Evidence and Knowledge processes with delayed messages, defines a ConsistencyContract such as Eventually: EvidencePublished -> KnowledgeAvailable, i.e. PublishedFact ⇒ EventuallyVisible under the explicit assumption MessageInfrastructureEventuallyRecovers; if recovery never happens the system must eventually expose IntegrationFailure rather than silently continuing to claim Synchronized. Introduces IntegrationState in {Healthy, Delayed, Degraded, Failed} as valuable operational knowledge, and compositional observability: the system should answer 'which boundary is preventing this workflow from progressing' (e.g. Decision -> WaitingForAuthorization because GovernanceContext=Unavailable) via an explicit BlockedBecause(X) -- 'not merely monitoring... part of the explainability of workflow state'.

a_rows_sample.anchor: EvidenceGraph vs ExecutionGraph: 'why do we believe this' != 'what happened operationally'
a_rows_sample.statement: Gives two complementary explanation chains: Decision -> KnowledgeSnapshot -> Claims -> Evidence (the EvidenceGraph, answering 'why do we believe this') and Decision -> Authorization -> Action -> Outcome (the ExecutionGraph, answering 'what happened operationally') -- 'these graphs must not be merged blindly'; they intersect but are not identical.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Compositional-correctness matrix; two intentionally-discovered hazards; discovery-of-failure as the intended scientific outcome
a_rows_sample.statement: Tabulates eleven compositions with their main risk and result (Evidence->Knowledge: identity/provenance, PASS; Knowledge->Decision: snapshot drift, corrected; Decision->Governance: policy drift, PASS; Governance->Action: authorization race, corrected; Action->Outcome: wrong correlation, PASS; Learning->Knowledge: direct mutation, PASS; Agent->Decision: concurrency, PASS; Eventual consistency: false absence, PASS; Semantic translation: semantic inflation, PASS; Evidence->Causal: false causality, PASS; Context dependency: circular dependency, PASS), noting two intentionally discovered and corrected hazards (mutable knowledge reference; authorization TOCTOU race). States the important scientific conclusion: discovering these failures is good -- the goal is not 100% PASS by avoiding difficult tests but finding counterexamples, per the loop Find failure -> understand failure -> strengthen invariant/contract -> rerun.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Provisional KnowledgeOS Compositionality Principle (six conditions) -- a design hypothesis, not a proven theorem
a_rows_sample.statement: Formulates a provisional KnowledgeOS Compositionality Principle: if (1) each context preserves its local invariants, (2) every cross-context interaction uses an explicit contract, (3) semantic translations preserve required meaning, (4) immutable/versioned references are used for historical state, (5) authorization is valid at the point of side effect, and (6) integration failures are represented explicitly, then LocalCorrectness + ContractCorrectness ⇒ RelevantGlobalCorrectness -- explicitly flagged as 'not yet a formal mathematical theorem for all possible KnowledgeOS implementations... a design theorem/hypothesis that we can continue to test'.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Step 58 verdict PASS WITH CORRECTIONS; opens Step 59 on concurrency and operation commutativity
a_rows_sample.statement: Declares STEP 58 -- PASS WITH CORRECTIONS ('stronger than simply PASS'), naming the two discovered hazards (mutable knowledge reference -> historical contamination; AuthorizationCheck(t1)->Execute(t2) -> possible authorization race) as architecture behaving 'increasingly like a real engineering system rather than a conceptual framework': Local Safety + Local Liveness + CrossContext Contracts + Compositional Safety. Identifies the remaining gap: reasoning has so far been single-execution-history; real KnowledgeOS will have N>>1 simultaneous operations, so Step 59 (Concurrency and Interleaving Calculus) will model simultaneous workflows W_1,...,W_n and their interleavings, asking whether individually valid transitions in different orders produce the same valid result -- the central commutativity question T_a(T_b(X)) = T_b(T_a(X))? -- and where operations do not commute, requiring explicit Ordering, Locking, Versioning, ConflictResolution, or DomainPolicy, 'before we can make a serious claim that the KnowledgeOS architecture is computationally robust, rather than merely logically coherent'.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Experiments 6-10: concurrent authorization/revocation TOCTOU reinforced; explicit PolicySelectionRule required; snapshot isolation for concurrent evidence arrival; simultaneous learning kept as separate candidate revisions pending explicit Merge; multi-agent proposals with no-majority-truth-assumption
a_rows_sample.statement: Experiment 6: Authorize(D1,t1) followed by RevokeAuthority(t2), execution at t3 requires AuthorizationValid(t3), else fail/reauthorize -- PASS, 'reinforces the Step 58 correction'. Experiment 7: concurrent P1 active / P2 published during an in-flight decision request requires an explicit PolicySelectionRule (not 'whichever database row happens to be current'), with candidate semantics PolicyAtRequestTime / PolicyAtDecisionTime / PolicyAtAuthorizationTime, domain-dependent but must be explicit -- PASS, generalizing to 'whenever we see current, ask: current relative to what time?'. Experiment 8: evidence E1 arriving after Snapshot(D1)=K_t is established cannot silently enter that historical snapshot (belongs to K_{t+1} or later) -- PASS, 'an epistemic form of snapshot isolation: decision sees a defined knowledge state, later information does not retroactively modify it'. Experiment 9: two simultaneous learning processes proposing K_{t+1}^A and K_{t+1}^B must not overwrite one another -- both CandidateRevision_A and CandidateRevision_B remain separately identifiable, with Merge(K_A,K_B) as an explicit domain operation, never implicit -- PASS. Experiment 10: three agents' independent proposals P1,P2,P3 are all stored independently for later domain evaluation -- PASS, 'exactly the architecture we want for multi-agent systems' -- with the explicit warning that P1=P2!=P3 (2:1 agreement) must not be inferred as P1=True merely by majority: agent agreement is evidence about agreement, not automatically evidence about truth; combining multiple independent estimates statistically requires an explicit AggregationModel, not simple majority.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Non-separable organizational utility with interaction terms; individually-optimal-collectively-bad experiments
b_rows_sample.statement: States LocalCorrectness ⇏ GlobalCorrectness at the multi-agent level: agents individually optimizing speed/cost/quality can each be locally optimal while U_org(a1*,a2*,a3*) is low. Experiment 1: two individually-optimal agent decisions jointly create a production bottleneck -- LocalOptimality=True, SystemOptimality=False -- PASS. Formalizes U_org = sum_i U_i(a_i) + sum_{i,j} I_ij(a_i,a_j), where interaction terms I_ij represent effects of action combinations -- 'where systemic behavior emerges'. Experiment 2: U1(A)=100, U2(B)=100 but I_12(A,B)=-250 gives U_org(A,B)=-50 -- LocalSuccess, SystemFailure -- PASS.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Aggregate resource/risk constraints; IndividualFeasibility ⇏ CollectiveFeasibility
b_rows_sample.statement: Requires aggregate constraints over collective actions, e.g. sum_i Risk(a_i) <= R_max applying to system state, not one decision. Experiment 3: 50 individually-safe deployments jointly exceed R_max -- LocalInvariants=True, GlobalInvariant=False -- PASS. Experiment 4: each action individually satisfying Risk(a_i)<=r but their sum exceeding R_max requires some actions to be blocked or coordinated -- PASS. Gives IndividualFeasibility ⇏ CollectiveFeasibility via a resource example (three 40-unit requests against 100 capacity, each individually approved but jointly exceeding it); experiment 5 confirms SystemConstraintViolation -- PASS.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Global invariant over organizational state; coordination as a first-class, not-necessarily-centralized concept
b_rows_sample.statement: Formalizes global state S=(S_1,...,S_n) with I(S)=True required to be preserved by governed transitions (I(S)=True ⇒ I(S')=True). Experiment 6: an agent action producing S' with I(S')=False is TransitionRejected or Escalated -- PASS. Experiment 7: a locally-successful agent transaction leaving I_global false is LocalCommit ≠ GlobalSuccess -- PASS. Requires a coordination mechanism to detect PotentialInteraction(a_i,a_j) via ResourceLock/Reservation/GlobalConstraintCheck/CoordinationProtocol/Saga/Compensation, domain-dependent. Experiment 8: two agents performing incompatible simultaneous operations with no coordination yields ConflictDetection/ExecutionBlocked -- PASS. Explicitly rejects assuming coordination requires centralization: distributed mechanisms (leases, reservations, event protocols, consensus, constraint services, workflow orchestration) suffice. Experiment 9: requiring every organizational decision to pass through one AI coordinator is NotRequired (bottleneck, single point of failure, governance concentration, scalability limitation) -- PASS.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Organizational feedback dynamics and stability; planning horizon and short-term-vs-long-term optimal decisions
b_rows_sample.statement: Formalizes the organization as a dynamical system S_{t+1}=F(S_t,pi(S_t)) via A_t=pi(S_t). Experiment 10: a resource-allocation/demand/quality positive-feedback loop yields FeedbackDetected -- PASS. Poses organizational stability as a formal question analogous to x_{t+1}=f(x_t); experiment 11: x_{t+1}=1.2x_t growing 100->120->144->172.8 is UnstableGrowth -- PASS, requiring evaluation of LongTermSystemBehavior via simulation/scenario analysis. Experiment 12: one-step-optimal action performing substantially worse over 20 iterations gives ShortTermOptimal != LongTermOptimal -- PASS. Introduces planning horizon H with EU_{0:H} = sum_{t=0}^{H} gamma^t R_t (gamma = time preference/discount), making the horizon part of the decision model. Experiment 13: whether action A (immediate-utility-maximizing) or B (long-term-superior) is chosen depends on the declared horizon -- PASS.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Systemic risk under correlation; common-mode risk via dependency-graph centrality; Centrality != Risk
b_rows_sample.statement: States correlated risks can produce P(A∩B) >> P(A)P(B), so risk cannot always be summed independently. Experiment 14: assuming independent agent risks when they actually share infrastructure yields CorrelationRisk -- PASS. Restates common-mode failure at organizational scale (A1,A2,A3 all depending on Infrastructure_X); experiment 15: three seemingly independent agents sharing one database all failing together yields SystemicDependencyDetected -- PASS. Uses the existing dependency graph G_D for systemic-risk analysis: high node Centrality suggests high failure impact -- experiment 16 detects a hidden central dependency (twenty agents all depending on Service_X) as CriticalDependency -- PASS. But warns Centrality != Risk: a highly connected but redundant node need not be risky -- Risk requires Dependency + FailureProbability + Impact + Recoverability. Experiment 17: a high-centrality Service_X with three redundant replicas yields CentralityHigh but only moderate SystemicRisk -- PASS.

b_rows_sample.anchor: CollectiveFailure defined; four-tier invariant hierarchy (local/domain/organizational/constitutional) mapped onto layered architecture
b_rows_sample.statement: Defines CollectiveFailure as I_global(S)=False even though every individual I_i(S_i)=True. Experiment 18: all-agents-locally-valid but I_global=False yields CollectiveFailure -- PASS. Gives a four-tier invariant hierarchy I_local, I_domain, I_organizational, I_constitutional, with ValidAction = AND_k I_k across all applicable levels. Experiment 19: an action satisfying I_local but violating I_organizational is ActionRejected -- PASS. Maps this onto the layered architecture Constitution -> Governance -> Domain -> Application -> Infrastructure, paralleling I_constitutional -> I_organizational -> I_domain -> I_local -- 'the mathematical invariant hierarchy maps naturally onto DDD and software architecture'.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Emergence != Failure; governable emergent behavior requires system-level (not merely per-agent) observability
b_rows_sample.statement: States Emergence != Failure: complex systems can produce desirable emergent behavior; the requirement is that emergent behavior be observable, bounded, and governable where it matters. Experiment 20: agents independently cooperating to produce a beneficial emergent pattern with no central plan is Allowed provided global invariants remain satisfied -- PASS, 'avoids over-centralizing KnowledgeOS'. Requires SystemObservation (not only per-agent AgentObservation_i): experiment 21 shows that when all agents expose telemetry but no aggregate system state exists, a systemic failure can emerge undetected -- SystemObservabilityGap -- PASS.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Organizational state as an irreducible aggregate; collective action-set optimization
b_rows_sample.statement: Defines S_org = Aggregate(S_1,...,S_n, Resources, Policies, Dependencies, ExternalState) -- 'organization has a state that is not reducible to one agent's state'. Gives the transition S_org,t --ActionSet--> S_org,t+1 for a collective action set A_t={a_1,...,a_n}, which must satisfy global invariants. Experiment 22: an individually-valid action set that is globally invalid is ActionSetRejected or decomposed into a safe subset -- PASS. Reformulates the optimization problem as max_{A_t} U_org(A_t) subject to I_global(S_{t+1})=True (not just max_a U(a) for one agent) -- 'the mathematical foundation of coordinated agent execution', noting this optimization can itself be distributed, not necessarily centralized. Experiment 23: among three feasible action sets, only A2 maximizes global utility while preserving global invariants, and A2 is correctly selected -- PASS.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Collective-decision provenance/audit requirement
b_rows_sample.statement: Requires a collective decision D_org to trace lineage to constituent decisions D_1,...,D_n plus a DecisionProtocol. Experiment 24: a collective decision with no record of participants, votes, quorum, protocol, or evidence is CollectiveDecisionAuditIncomplete -- PASS.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Fault vs Causality separation: CausalContribution != OrganizationalResponsibility; five distinct accountability relations
b_rows_sample.statement: Poses the collective-responsibility question and rejects inferring responsibility merely from causal contribution: CausalContribution != OrganizationalResponsibility. Experiment 25: an agent that technically contributed to a failure while following authorized policy/valid protocol/its assigned responsibility boundary has CausalContribution=True without Fault=True -- PASS, 'extremely important in governance'. Requires five distinct, non-collapsible relations: Caused, ContributedTo, ResponsibleFor, ViolatedPolicy, Negligent. Experiment 26: an action causally contributing to an incident without violating any policy yields CausalContribution=True, PolicyViolation=False -- PASS. Concludes the organization is CausalStructure + ResponsibilityStructure + AuthorityStructure + KnowledgeStructure -- intersecting but semantically distinct structures, 'a powerful DDD result'.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Unified system-state equation, complete organizational loop, and four new invariants (I_Collective, I_SystemObservation, I_Interaction, I_ResponsibilitySeparation)
b_rows_sample.statement: Gives the unified system-state equation S_{t+1} = F(S_t, A_1,...,A_n, External_t), each A_i constrained by Capability_i, Authority_i, Policy_i, Responsibility_i, with the collective action required to satisfy I_global(S_{t+1})=True. Gives the complete organizational loop: Observe -> Knowledge -> CausalModel -> IndividualDecision -> Coordination -> CollectiveDecision -> Authorization -> ActionSet -> SystemOutcome -> Evaluation -> Learning. Adds four invariants: I_Collective (locally valid actions must not be considered collectively valid until required global invariants are evaluated); I_SystemObservation (material organizational invariants must be observable at the system level); I_Interaction (where actions interact, their joint effects must be evaluated rather than assuming separability); I_ResponsibilitySeparation (causal contribution, authority, policy compliance, and organizational responsibility must remain distinct concepts).

b_rows_sample.anchor: Step 79 verdict: KnowledgeOS must govern the system formed by interacting agents; opens Step 80 on organizational control and feedback
b_rows_sample.statement: Declares STEP 79 -- PASS: KnowledgeOS cannot be merely an agent platform -- it must represent and govern the behavior of the system formed by interacting agents, reframing the real object of the architecture as Human + AI + Software + Knowledge + Governance + Environment. Opens Step 80 (Organizational Control and Feedback): whether KnowledgeOS can keep an organization within desired boundaries over time, drawing on control theory (State, Observation, Control, Feedback, Stability, Drift, Thresholds, EarlyWarning, AdaptiveControl) -- centrally, how KnowledgeOS should react when the organization's real state gradually drifts from its governed architecture, framed as detecting and governing architectural drift continuously rather than designing a correct architecture once.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Concrete architecture-boundary-erosion example identified as the Step-79 systemic/emergent phenomenon; LocalCompliance⇏ArchitecturalIntegrity (Experiment 21)
b_rows_sample.statement: Gives a worked example: approved architecture specifies Service->DomainAPI, but over time developers individually introduce Service->Database, then Service->LegacyService, then Service->SharedUtility; each change may individually appear harmless, but collectively they produce ArchitectureBoundaryViolation -- explicitly identified as 'exactly the systemic behavior from Step 79'. Each developer action may satisfy local coding rules yet GlobalArchitectureInvariant=False, giving LocalCompliance⇏ArchitecturalIntegrity. Experiment 21: every pull request passes CodingStandard, every service passes UnitTests, but the dependency graph violates LayeringInvariant -- expected ArchitectureViolation -- PASS.

b_aliases: Step 79 Emergence, Systemic Risk, and Collective Correctness

group_evidence.why_grouped: explicit agent-stated uncertainty: 'kos-emergence-systemic-risk-collective-correctness' POSSIBLY relates to 'compositional-correctness-and-proof-boundaries' (batch B0023). Note: Step 79's collective/organizational-scale extension of compositional correctness: non-separable interaction-term utility, aggregate resource/risk constraints, coordination without centralization, organizational feedback stability and planning-horizon-dependent decisions, correlated systemic risk with dependency-centrality analysis, the four-tier invariant hierarchy, Emergence≠Failure with system-level observability, organizational state as an irreducible aggregate, collective action-set optimization, and the Fault-vs-Causality/five-relation responsibility separation. Extends compositional-correctness-and-proof-boundaries (Steps 48/58/71) from bounded-context composition to multi-agent/organizational composition.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Steps 82-88 asked what can we know, infer, predict, aggregate, preserve. Step 89 asks what can actually be computed. Knowledge ≠ Computability ≠ Feasibility.
a_rows_sample.statement: Introduces Step 89's central distinction Knowledge ≠ Computability ≠ Feasibility: information can be True while Computability is False, or a computable answer may still be operationally infeasible.

a_rows_sample.anchor: 89.1 — Three different failures ... Case A Missing information: InformationInsufficient. Case B Undecidable: NoGeneralAlgorithm. Case C Computationally infeasible: algorithm exists but too expensive. Unknown, Undecidable, Intractable must not be represented as the same state.
a_rows_sample.statement: Defines three distinct failure modes when a question cannot be answered: Case A InformationInsufficient (Unknown), Case B NoGeneralAlgorithm (Undecidable), Case C too-expensive-to-compute (Intractable) — none may be conflated.

a_rows_sample.anchor: 89.2 — Experiment 1 ... 'Was system X compliant?' KnowledgeOS has not retrieved the relevant policy. Expected: Unknown rather than False. Result: PASS
a_rows_sample.statement: Experiment 1: a compliance question with unretrieved policy must yield Unknown, not False; result PASS.

a_rows_sample.anchor: 89.3 — Experiment 2 ... Question is theoretically undecidable for arbitrary programs. KnowledgeOS fails to produce an answer. Expected: Undecidable rather than Unknown. Result: PASS
a_rows_sample.statement: Experiment 2: a theoretically undecidable question must be labeled Undecidable, not merely Unknown; result PASS.

a_rows_sample.anchor: 89.4 — Experiment 3 ... A problem has an algorithm but requires 2^100 operations. KnowledgeOS does not compute it. Expected: ComputationallyInfeasible rather than Undecidable. Result: PASS
a_rows_sample.statement: Experiment 3: a decidable-but-2^100-operation problem must be labeled ComputationallyInfeasible, not Undecidable; result PASS.

a_rows_sample.anchor: 89.5 — Decidability ... a decision problem is decidable if there exists an algorithm that accepts every valid input, terminates, and returns the correct answer. f:X→{0,1}, exists A such that A(x)=f(x) and T_A(x)<∞ for every valid x.
a_rows_sample.statement: Formally defines decidability: f:X→{0,1} is decidable if an algorithm A exists with A(x)=f(x) and finite runtime T_A(x) for every valid x.

a_rows_sample.anchor: 89.6 — Experiment 4 ... KnowledgeOS checks a finite set of explicit rules R_1..R_n. Each rule terminates. Expected: compliance checking is decidable for that formalized rule set. Result: PASS
a_rows_sample.statement: Experiment 4: checking a finite set of terminating rules is decidable; result PASS.

a_rows_sample.anchor: 89.7 — Finite-state systems ... S={s_1..s_n}. Transitions T⊆S×A×S. Questions such as 'can state s_bad ever be reached?' can often be solved algorithmically.
a_rows_sample.statement: Proposes reducing engineering governance questions to finite-state systems S with transitions T⊆S×A×S, enabling algorithmic reachability questions.

a_rows_sample.anchor: 89.8 — Experiment 5 ... System has 100 finite states. A model checker evaluates all reachable states. Expected: Reachability is decidable. Result: PASS
a_rows_sample.statement: Experiment 5: model-checking a 100-state system confirms reachability is decidable; result PASS.

a_rows_sample.anchor: 89.9 — This is highly relevant to KnowledgeOS ... S_0-A_1->S_1-A_2->S_2. UnauthorizedDeployment ∉ ReachableStates could become a formal property.
a_rows_sample.statement: Proposes formalizing governance as explicit state transitions so that properties like UnauthorizedDeployment ∉ ReachableStates become formally verifiable.

a_rows_sample.anchor: 89.10 — Experiment 6 ... ApprovalRequired before ProductionDeployment. Formal transition model contains no transition Unapproved→Production. Expected: the model can formally establish that the transition is impossible within the model. Result: PASS
a_rows_sample.statement: Experiment 6: a formal transition model lacking an Unapproved→Production transition formally establishes that transition is impossible within the model; result PASS.

a_rows_sample.anchor: 89.11 — Important qualification ... Formal verification proves Property(Model)=True. It does not automatically prove Property(Reality)=True. If the model omits a bypass path, the proof may be irrelevant to reality.
a_rows_sample.statement: Warns that formal verification proves Property(Model)=True, not automatically Property(Reality)=True; a model omitting a real bypass path makes the proof irrelevant to reality.

a_rows_sample.anchor: 89.12 — Experiment 7 ... Formal model proves UnauthorizedDeployment=False. But a manually accessible production server exists outside the model. Expected: ModelCorrect but SystemAssuranceIncomplete. Result: PASS. This connects directly to Step 85's governance-surface concept.
a_rows_sample.statement: Experiment 7: a correct formal proof (UnauthorizedDeployment=False) alongside an out-of-model manual bypass server is ModelCorrect but SystemAssuranceIncomplete; result PASS; explicitly linked to Step 85/86's governance-surface concept.

a_rows_sample.anchor: 89.13 — Verification versus validation ... Verification: did we build the system according to its formal specification? Validation: does the specification/model actually represent the real system adequately? Both are necessary.
a_rows_sample.statement: Distinguishes Verification (built according to formal spec) from Validation (spec adequately represents reality); both are necessary.

a_rows_sample.anchor: 89.14 — Experiment 8 ... Model is internally consistent but represents the wrong business process. Expected: Verification=True but Validation=False. Result: PASS
a_rows_sample.statement: Experiment 8: an internally consistent model of the wrong business process shows Verification=True but Validation=False; result PASS.

a_rows_sample.anchor: 89.15 — The halting problem ... Given arbitrary program P and input x, will P(x) eventually terminate? is undecidable in general. There is no algorithm H(P,x) that correctly answers this for all programs and always terminates.
a_rows_sample.statement: States the halting problem: no algorithm H(P,x) decides termination correctly for all programs and always terminates.

a_rows_sample.anchor: 89.16 — Experiment 9 ... 'Will every arbitrary program eventually terminate?' Expected: UndecidableInGeneral. Result: PASS
a_rows_sample.statement: Experiment 9: the general termination question is UndecidableInGeneral; result PASS.

a_rows_sample.anchor: 89.17 — Why this matters ... We should never design KnowledgeOS around the assumption EveryQuestion→DefinitiveAnswer. Some questions have NoGeneralAlgorithmicAnswer.
a_rows_sample.statement: Draws the design lesson: KnowledgeOS must never be designed around EveryQuestion→DefinitiveAnswer, since some questions have NoGeneralAlgorithmicAnswer.

a_rows_sample.anchor: 89.18 — But restricted domains can be decidable ... FiniteStatePrograms termination can often be decided. UndecidableGeneralProblem does not imply UndecidableEveryRestrictedInstance.
a_rows_sample.statement: States UndecidableGeneralProblem does not imply UndecidableEveryRestrictedInstance: restricting to finite-state programs can restore decidability of termination.

a_rows_sample.anchor: 89.19 — Experiment 10 ... General program termination: Undecidable. Finite-state workflow termination: Decidable. Expected: KnowledgeOS distinguishes the domains. Result: PASS
a_rows_sample.statement: Experiment 10: KnowledgeOS must distinguish undecidable general-program termination from decidable finite-state workflow termination; result PASS.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Global invariant I_global(S); reachable-states quantification; safety versus liveness
b_rows_sample.statement: Defines a global invariant I_global(S) required for every valid system state S, with the architectural objective for-all S in ReachableStates: I_global(S)=True (not every imaginable state, only validly reachable ones, via Reach(KOS,S_0)). Distinguishes Safety ('something bad never happens', e.g. UnauthorizedAction ⇒ not-Executed) from Liveness ('something good eventually happens', e.g. SubmittedRevision ⇒ Eventually(ProcessedRevision)); a system that never decides is safe but useless, so Safety alone is insufficient -- KnowledgeOS needs Safety + Liveness + EpistemicIntegrity + Traceability.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Error propagation versus containment; fail-safe is not universally fail-closed; risk-weighted assurance
b_rows_sample.statement: Distinguishes errors that must propagate (CriticalEvidenceInvalid -> DecisionReevaluation) from errors that should be contained (MalformedOptionalMetadata -> RejectMetadata), requiring explicit error semantics. For critical authorization, Unknown -> Block may be appropriate; for noncritical informational features, Unknown -> ContinueWithWarning may be acceptable, so FailurePolicy is part of the domain/governance contract -- fail-safe is not universally 'fail closed': a global AllFailures -> Block rule would make the system impractical; correct behavior depends on Risk and DecisionType. Formalizes risk-weighted assurance AssuranceRequired = f(R(d)), with higher risk requiring stronger assurance, and argues formal-verification effort should itself be risk-weighted (strong guarantees for authorization/security/financial transitions/election integrity/production changes, not every UI label) -- 'pragmatic formal engineering'.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Correctness as a multi-dimensional property: safety, liveness, fairness, deadlock, consistency (strong vs eventual)
b_rows_sample.statement: Writes a safety property as not-BadState for all reachable states and a liveness property as Request ⇒ Eventually(Response) under stated assumptions; adds fairness (ValidRequest ⇒ EventuallyProcessed given available resources) and notes deadlock as a case where Safety=True but Liveness=False (Decision_A waits for Decision_B which waits for A). Defines Correctness = {Safety, Liveness, Consistency, Traceability, EpistemicIntegrity, GovernanceCompliance}, not merely 'NoBug'. For consistency, distinguishes StrongConsistency from EventualConsistency (example: an audit record needs Strong, a search index may tolerate Eventual), so each invariant should carry an explicit ConsistencyRequirement (e.g. I_audit=Strong, I_search=Eventual); Conflict(C1,C2) between contradictory same-object claims must become explicit knowledge rather than silently resolved.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Invariant registry artifact and verification-method taxonomy with sound abstraction
b_rows_sample.statement: Defines an InvariantRegistry artifact where each invariant carries ID, owner bounded context, formal statement, criticality, enforcement point, verification method, failure policy, evidence, version, and status (worked example: INV-GOV-001, 'Production execution requires valid authorization', owned by Governance Context, Critical, enforced at the Decision Gate, verified by formal rule + integration test, failure=Block execution, v1.0); every invariant needs exactly one authoritative owner, preventing MultipleContexts -> ConflictingTruth. Lists verification methods (FormalProof, ModelChecking, PropertyBasedTest, IntegrationTest, RuntimeAssertion, HumanReview) with differing assurance levels, and defense-in-depth enforcement across Domain -> Application -> Infrastructure -> Runtime layers that must not create contradictory semantics. For property-based testing/model checking, notes state-space explosion (|Reach| can grow exponentially) requiring abstraction: alpha: ConcreteState -> AbstractState, with a sound abstraction requiring Violation_Concrete ⇒ Violation_Abstract for the property verified ('a key formal-methods principle') -- concluding KnowledgeOS does not need a theorem prover everywhere, but can combine FormalMethods + DeterministicRules + PropertyTests + StatisticalValidation + RuntimeChecks + Governance.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Layered correctness and the first candidate KOSCorrect predicate
b_rows_sample.statement: Defines Correctness = C_formal ∩ C_deterministic ∩ C_empirical ∩ C_epistemic ∩ C_governance -- 'a system can be mathematically correct but operationally invalid if governance is wrong'. Formulates the first candidate correctness contract: KOSCorrect iff I_global ∧ Contracts ∧ Safety ∧ Liveness ∧ Traceability ∧ EpistemicIntegrity, explicitly caveated as 'not yet a machine-checkable theorem... our architectural correctness specification'; the document explicitly warns against claiming KnowledgeOS 'has now been mathematically proven correct' -- the correct statement is that a candidate formal specification now exists against which correctness can be demonstrated.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Twelve falsification experiments for Step 48 global-invariant/correctness model (all PASS)
b_rows_sample.statement: Runs twelve falsification tests, all PASS: (1) a component is locally correct but its interface translation violates semantics => global invariant failure detected; (2) all safety properties hold but a workflow deadlocks => safety passes, liveness fails; (3) evidence is modified without a new version => evidence-integrity violation; (4) a decision uses a model created after the decision date => temporal/historical-integrity violation; (5) an AI proposal bypasses authorization => AI-boundary and authorization invariants fail; (6) a causal claim has no documented assumptions => causal-integrity violation; (7) a trusted claim becomes invalid but remains operational without review => revision/invalidation-invariant violation; (8) a safety-critical unknown is treated as true => unknown-state/safety-invariant violation; (9) a claim valid in one bounded context is applied to another without semantic mapping => scope/semantic-integrity violation; (10) two distributed replicas temporarily disagree where eventual consistency is permitted => no violation if the declared consistency contract allows it; (11) two replicas disagree on a strong-consistency invariant => critical consistency violation; (12) a model is stable and highly confident but external validation shows systematic error => epistemic correctness fails despite model stability.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Three-level distinction: MathematicalConsistency / ReferenceMachineConsistency / ProductionSystemCorrectness; PASS != production-proven
b_rows_sample.statement: Issues a scientific correction on the word PASS: these are formal reference-machine experiments, not evidence a production implementation has passed. Establishes 'the specified machine has a coherent execution path under the tested scenarios' but explicitly not ProductionImplementationCorrect. Introduces three levels: Level 1 MathematicalConsistency (tested in Steps 49-50); Level 2 ReferenceMachineConsistency (specified and exercised in Steps 51/56); Level 3 ProductionSystemCorrectness (not yet demonstrated) -- 'this distinction is extremely important'.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Precise falsification criterion for safety □I(X_t) and liveness ◇Goal; safety evidence currently stronger than liveness evidence
b_rows_sample.statement: Gives a precise falsification criterion: finding X_t with I(X_t)=True where a valid transition produces I(X_{t+1})=False would be a genuine architectural failure; finding a ValidDomainState with no valid transition despite the domain requiring progress would expose a liveness defect. Formalizes Safety as Box I(X_t) (something bad never happens) and Liveness as Diamond Goal (something good eventually happens), and states KnowledgeOS currently has substantially stronger evidence for safety than for liveness -- 'an important scientific qualification'. Illustrates the liveness gap: a system can preserve every invariant and still get stuck in Decision -> Waiting -> Waiting -> Waiting with no invariant violated, yet the workflow has failed.

b_rows_sample.anchor: 89.13 — Verification versus validation ... Verification: did we build the system according to its formal specification? Validation: does the specification/model actually represent the real system adequately? Both are necessary.
b_rows_sample.statement: Distinguishes Verification (built according to formal spec) from Validation (spec adequately represents reality); both are necessary.

b_rows_sample.anchor: 89.14 — Experiment 8 ... Model is internally consistent but represents the wrong business process. Expected: Verification=True but Validation=False. Result: PASS
b_rows_sample.statement: Experiment 8: an internally consistent model of the wrong business process shows Verification=True but Validation=False; result PASS.

group_evidence.why_grouped: explicit agent-stated uncertainty: 'computability-decidability-limits-model' POSSIBLY relates to 'formal-verification-strategy-model' (batch B0024). Note: Step 89: separates Knowledge!=Computability!=Feasibility and Unknown/Undecidable/Infeasible as non-conflatable failure modes. Closely related to the pre-existing formal-verification-strategy-model.
