a_rows_sample.anchor: Concurrent-composition safety; optimistic versioning and revalidation
a_rows_sample.statement: Shows local invariant satisfaction is insufficient under concurrency: D1 and D2 both independently satisfy I(S_t) but execute simultaneously, and the combined S_{t+2} may violate I(S_{t+2}) -- requiring ConcurrentCompositionSafety. Proposes optimistic concurrency: Version(S_t)=v, a decision operates against v, and if the state has advanced to v+1 the action requires Revalidate(D); formal rule: Execute(D) requires Version(CurrentState)=Version(Snapshot(D)), else Revalidate(D) -- 'a very strong rule for critical state transitions', naturally building on the existing DecisionSnapshot construct.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Idempotency invariant against retry; ActionID uniqueness
a_rows_sample.statement: If Execute(A) succeeds but the response is lost and the client retries, without idempotency A may execute twice, so ActionID must be unique; states the idempotency invariant Execute(x) x n => EffectiveExecution(x)=1 for a critical action with ActionID=x.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Event ordering requirement; partial-failure PartialCompletion state; four-valued OutcomeStatus
a_rows_sample.statement: If E1 must precede E2 but E2 arrives first, the system must buffer, reject, reconcile, or apply a valid commutative rule -- it must not silently produce an invalid state. If an action updates system A but fails before system B, State_A != State_B and KnowledgeOS must represent PartialCompletion rather than recording Success as if everything completed; introduces OutcomeStatus in {Success, Failure, Partial, Unknown}, 'more accurate than binary Success/Failure'.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Unknown outcome and 'absence of confirmation != confirmation of absence'
a_rows_sample.statement: If connectivity is lost after submitting an action, the correct state is UnknownOutcome, neither Failure nor Success. States the powerful invariant: absence of confirmation != confirmation of absence, formally not-Observed(Success) ⇏ Observed(Failure). Extends the reference Outcome domain to Outcome=(ActionID, Status, Observation, Timestamp, Evidence).

a_rows_sample.anchor: Replay: StateReplay != ActionReplay; functional core / imperative shell
a_rows_sample.statement: Requires Replay(E1,...,En)=S_n for deterministic state reconstruction, but warns external-world effects (e.g. SendEmail) cannot safely be re-executed merely because an event is replayed -- StateReplay != ActionReplay, 'crucial'. This motivates an explicit PureTransition versus SideEffect distinction, mapping onto a Functional Core (deterministic state transformations) / Imperative Shell (external actions) software architecture: 'pure reasoning + controlled side effects', keeping the mathematical engine deterministic even when the external world is not, 'substantially easier' to verify. Depicts a reference architecture: KnowledgeOS Mathematical Core (State/Rules/Inference/Invariant) -> Decision -> Policy/Gate -> Action -> External World -> Outcome -> Observation/Event.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Attacks 28-38: deadlock, starvation, BC leakage, aggregate bypass, duplicate/out-of-order events, replay, nondeterministic AI, corrupted model registry, provenance vs causal cycles (all PASS; several new mandatory contracts surfaced)
a_rows_sample.statement: Attack 28 deadlock (A waits for B, B waits for A): Safety may hold while Liveness fails -- PASS, the safety/liveness distinction survives. Attack 29 starvation (a valid request perpetually postponed): Safety=True, Liveness=False, must be detected at workflow/governance level -- PASS. Attack 30 bounded-context leakage (Context A directly manipulates Context B's internal state, bypassing B's invariants): must be prohibited -- PASS assuming boundary enforcement. Attack 31 aggregate invariant bypass (external service modifies aggregate internals without the domain operation): AggregateState must be modified only through controlled transitions -- PASS. Attack 32 duplicate events (Event(E) delivered twice): non-idempotent processing yields WrongState, so critical event handlers require Idempotency -- PASS, surfacing the new mandatory contract that CriticalEventProcessing must define duplicate handling. Attack 33 out-of-order events (E2 before E1): requires explicit event ordering/version semantics to prevent incorrect state reconstruction -- PASS. Attack 34 full-history replay: Replay(H)=ReconstructedState, deterministically Replay(H)=S_t provided event semantics/versions are preserved -- PASS. Attack 35 nondeterministic AI decision (stochastic generation, non-byte-identical replay): does not invalidate the model; requires DecisionTrace rather than ByteIdenticalReplay -- PASS. Attack 36 corrupted model registry (metadata says Version=5, artifact is actually version 4): ModelIdentityIntegrity fails, requiring model identity to be cryptographically or otherwise reliably bound to the artifact -- PASS, introducing a new implementation requirement. Attack 37 provenance cycle (C1->C2->C1): requires cycle semantics, preferably DAG for derivation graphs -- PASS with the constraint that derivation provenance is acyclic. Attack 38 causal cycle (A->B->A, e.g. feedback systems): causal cycles CAN be real, so DAG semantics must NOT be imposed globally on causality -- 'Provenance DAG != CausalGraph DAG', a crucial distinction -- PASS.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Attacks 39-50: semantic cycle, relation-type collapse, unknown propagation, false precision, p-value/multiple-testing/selection-bias/MNAR abuse, mid-execution policy/authority change, concurrent decisions (all PASS; relations must be typed and governed)
a_rows_sample.statement: Attack 39 semantic cycle (Term_A<->Term_B): unproblematic if it is simply an equivalence relation -- cycles mean different things per relation type -- PASS. Attack 40 relation collapse (storing (source,target,relation) with arbitrary relation strings weakens semantic guarantees): requires R in R_registered -- PASS, surfacing the mandatory contract that relations must be typed and governed. Attack 41 unknown propagation (C1=Unknown used downstream): cannot silently become True, requires explicit three-valued or richer logic -- PASS. Attack 42 false precision (evidence supports x in [0.6,0.8], AI outputs x=0.731842): must preserve UncertaintyRepresentation -- PASS. Attack 43 statistical-significance abuse (p<0.001, negligible effect size): must distinguish StatisticalSignificance from PracticalSignificance -- PASS. Attack 44 multiple testing (10,000 hypotheses, some significant by chance): RawPValue cannot automatically become EvidenceOfDiscovery, correction/multiple-testing context required -- PASS. Attack 45 selection bias (training data restricted to successful projects): estimates P(Y|X,Selected), cannot automatically generalize to P(Y|X) -- PASS provided sampling context is preserved. Attack 46 missing-not-at-random data (missingness depends on the unobserved value): must preserve MissingnessMechanism when relevant -- PASS at the model level. Attack 47 policy changes mid-execution (P1 at start, P2 during execution): requires an explicit PolicyBindingRule (PolicyAtStart, PolicyAtExecution, or an explicit transition policy) -- PASS, exposing a required governance decision. Attack 48 authority changes mid-execution: requires an explicit AuthorityBindingRule -- PASS. Attack 49 knowledge changes during decision execution (K_t running, K_{t+1} created by new evidence): a running decision cannot silently switch to K_{t+1} if reproducibility matters; requires KnowledgeSnapshot -- PASS. Attack 50 concurrent decisions on the same aggregate (D1, D2 individually satisfy the invariant but jointly violate it): local validation is insufficient, requires ConcurrencyControl -- PASS, revealing an important global implementation requirement.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Command semantics and idempotency key; commands may be rejected (Command != Event)
a_rows_sample.statement: A command should contain Intent + Target + Parameters + Actor + Correlation (example: AuthorizeDecision carries decisionId, requestedBy, reason, correlationId). A command does not guarantee a state transition -- Command -> Accepted or Command -> Rejected, reinforcing Command != Event. Commands with external side effects require an IdempotencyKey k, such that Execute(Command,k) repeated multiple times yields EffectiveExecution(k)=1.

a_rows_sample.anchor: We now move from refinement to the next major mathematical boundary ... S_t -a1||a2-> ?. Does the system remain mathematically correct under concurrent execution?
a_rows_sample.statement: Frames Step 92's central question: whether the system remains mathematically correct when multiple agents act concurrently (S_t --a1‖a2--> ?), beyond the earlier sequential transition model.

a_rows_sample.anchor: 92.1 — Sequential reasoning is insufficient ... Balance=100. Two agents simultaneously request -80 and -70. Sequentially one should be rejected. But if both read Balance=100 before either writes, both may conclude 100≥amount.
a_rows_sample.statement: Illustrates that sequential reasoning about a balance invariant is insufficient when two agents concurrently read the same value before either writes.

a_rows_sample.anchor: 92.2 — Experiment 1: race condition ... B=100. A reads 100, approves 80. B reads 100, approves 70. Expected invariant B≥0. Actual result may be B=-50. Result: PASS. Concurrency can violate an invariant even when every individual operation is locally correct.
a_rows_sample.statement: Experiment 1: two agents both reading B=100 and independently approving -80/-70 can produce B=-50, violating B≥0 despite each operation being locally correct; result PASS.

a_rows_sample.anchor: 92.3 — Local correctness versus concurrent correctness ... forall a_i: Correct(a_i) does not imply Correct(a_1‖...‖a_n).
a_rows_sample.statement: States LocalCorrectness ≠ ConcurrentCorrectness: ∀a_i: Correct(a_i) does not imply Correct(a_1‖...‖a_n).

a_rows_sample.anchor: 92.4 — Atomicity ... Read+Validate+Write becomes one indivisible transaction.
a_rows_sample.statement: Proposes atomicity as a solution: combining Read+Validate+Write into one indivisible transaction.

a_rows_sample.anchor: 92.5 — Experiment 2 ... T_A=(Read,Validate,Write). Transaction B concurrent. Database guarantees serializable execution. Expected: one transaction observes the updated state and is rejected if the invariant would otherwise fail. Result: PASS
a_rows_sample.statement: Experiment 2: under serializable execution, one of two concurrent atomic transactions is rejected if the invariant would otherwise fail; result PASS.

a_rows_sample.anchor: 92.6 — Atomicity is not the same as correctness ... Atomic(UpdateStatus) does not prove Authorized(UpdateStatus).
a_rows_sample.statement: States atomicity does not imply authorization correctness: Atomic(UpdateStatus) does not prove Authorized(UpdateStatus).

a_rows_sample.anchor: 92.7 — Experiment 3 ... Unauthorized actor executes an atomic Approve(). Expected: atomicity does not make the action legitimate. Result: PASS
a_rows_sample.statement: Experiment 3: an atomic Approve() executed by an unauthorized actor remains illegitimate despite atomicity; result PASS.

a_rows_sample.anchor: 92.8 — Transactional invariant ... I(S) ⇒ I(T(S)). This is exactly the invariant-preservation concept from Step 91 applied to concurrent execution.
a_rows_sample.statement: Applies Step 91's invariant-preservation concept to transactions: I(S) ⇒ I(T(S)) — if the invariant held before a transaction, it must hold afterward.

a_rows_sample.anchor: 92.9 — Experiment 4 ... Before transaction I=True. After transaction I=False. Expected: TransactionInvalid. Result: PASS
a_rows_sample.statement: Experiment 4: a transaction turning I=True into I=False is TransactionInvalid; result PASS.

a_rows_sample.anchor: 92.10 — Serializability ... A concurrent execution is serializable if its observable result is equivalent to some valid sequential ordering. T_1‖T_2 should correspond to T_1;T_2 or T_2;T_1.
a_rows_sample.statement: Defines serializability: a concurrent execution T_1‖T_2 is serializable if equivalent to some valid sequential ordering (T_1;T_2 or T_2;T_1).

a_rows_sample.anchor: 92.11 — Experiment 5 ... Two concurrent approvals produce a state that cannot be produced by any valid sequential ordering. Expected: NonSerializableExecution. Result: PASS. This is a serious correctness problem.
a_rows_sample.statement: Experiment 5: two concurrent approvals producing a state unreachable by any sequential ordering is NonSerializableExecution, called a serious correctness problem; result PASS.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Step 92 established concurrent/distributed correctness. But real systems fail ... Can KnowledgeOS recover from failure without creating a state that violates its mathematical model? Failure ⇏ Semantic Corruption.
b_rows_sample.statement: Frames Step 93's central requirement: Failure ⇏ Semantic Corruption — KnowledgeOS must recover from failure without violating its mathematical model.

b_rows_sample.anchor: 93.1 — Failure is part of the state space ... S_0 -a-> S_partial -failure-> S_f. The system must define whether S_f is valid.
b_rows_sample.statement: Extends the state model to include failure explicitly: S_0 --a--> S_partial --failure--> S_f, requiring the system to define whether S_f is valid.

b_rows_sample.anchor: 93.2 — Experiment 1: interrupted transition ... Submitted→Approved. Crash occurs after step 1 (create approval). State: ApprovalExists=True but Status=Submitted. Expected: the intermediate state must either be valid by design or recoverable. Result: PASS
b_rows_sample.statement: Experiment 1: a crash after only the first of three approval steps leaves ApprovalExists=True/Status=Submitted, which must be either valid-by-design or recoverable; result PASS.

b_rows_sample.anchor: 93.3 — Atomic transaction ... T=(createApproval,updateStatus,emitRequiredState). Failure can cause T→Rollback. The system returns to S_0.
b_rows_sample.statement: Defines wrapping the multi-step approval as one atomic transaction T so failure causes rollback to S_0.

b_rows_sample.anchor: 93.4 — Experiment 2 ... Transaction fails before commit. Expected: S_after=S_before. Result: PASS. This is the classical atomicity property.
b_rows_sample.statement: Experiment 2 confirms the classical atomicity property: a pre-commit failure leaves S_after=S_before; result PASS.

b_rows_sample.anchor: 93.5 — But not everything is transactional ... commits database state, sends an external email, crashes. The database can roll back only its own state. The external email cannot necessarily be recalled.
b_rows_sample.statement: Warns that non-transactional side effects (e.g. a sent email) cannot be rolled back along with the database, even though the database transaction can.

b_rows_sample.anchor: 93.6 — Experiment 3 ... Database says Approved=True. Email was sent 'request rejected.' Expected: system has inconsistent external observations. Result: PASS
b_rows_sample.statement: Experiment 3: a database recording Approved=True while an already-sent email said 'rejected' creates inconsistent external observations; result PASS.

b_rows_sample.anchor: 93.7 — Transaction boundary ... TransactionBoundary ≠ EntireRealWorld. A database transaction protects only the resources participating in it.
b_rows_sample.statement: States TransactionBoundary ≠ EntireRealWorld: a database transaction protects only its own participating resources, not external side effects.

b_rows_sample.anchor: 93.8 — Outbox pattern ... commit BusinessState+EventToPublish in the same local transaction. Then Outbox→MessageBroker. The external event is published after durable state exists.
b_rows_sample.statement: Describes the outbox pattern: committing BusinessState+EventToPublish atomically, then publishing from the outbox to a message broker after durable state exists.

b_rows_sample.anchor: 93.9 — Experiment 4 ... Transaction commits Approved=True and ApprovalEvent exists in an outbox. Process crashes before publication. Expected: recovery can publish the event later. Result: PASS
b_rows_sample.statement: Experiment 4: a crash before outbox event publication permits later recovery-driven publication; result PASS.

b_rows_sample.anchor: 93.10 — Durability ... Does committed state survive failure? If Commit(S_1) occurs, after restart we expect Recover()→S_1.
b_rows_sample.statement: Defines durability: committed state S_1 must be recoverable (Recover()→S_1) after a failure/restart.

b_rows_sample.anchor: 93.11 — Experiment 5 ... System confirms Commit=True. Power failure occurs immediately afterward. After restart: Status=Submitted. Expected: DurabilityViolation. Result: PASS
b_rows_sample.statement: Experiment 5: a confirmed commit reverting to Status=Submitted after a power failure is DurabilityViolation; result PASS.

b_rows_sample.anchor: 93.12 — Recovery function ... R(F,S) as the recovery process following failure F. We want R(F,S) ∈ ValidStates.
b_rows_sample.statement: Defines the recovery function R(F,S), requiring R(F,S) ∈ ValidStates.

b_rows_sample.anchor: 93.13 — Experiment 6 ... System crashes in an intermediate state. Recovery reconstructs a state satisfying I(S)=True. Expected: RecoveryCorrect. Result: PASS
b_rows_sample.statement: Experiment 6: recovery reconstructing a state satisfying I(S)=True from an intermediate crash is RecoveryCorrect; result PASS.

b_rows_sample.anchor: 93.14 — Recovery is a mathematical transition ... Recovery is not merely infrastructure. It is itself a transition S_failed-recover->S_recovered. Recovery must obey the same semantic invariants.
b_rows_sample.statement: States recovery is itself a mathematical transition S_failed --recover--> S_recovered, subject to the same semantic invariants as any other transition.

b_rows_sample.anchor: 93.15 — Experiment 7 ... Normal business transitions preserve I. Recovery process reconstructs state without checking I. Expected: potential invariant violation. Result: PASS
b_rows_sample.statement: Experiment 7: a recovery process that reconstructs state without checking invariant I risks invariant violation; result PASS.

b_rows_sample.anchor: 93.16 — Crash consistency ... state A,B,C. A transaction updates all three. A crash may occur between writes if atomicity is absent. If A'=A1,B'=B1,C'=C0 is impossible under the model, I(A',B',C')=False.
b_rows_sample.statement: Defines crash consistency: partial multi-field updates (A'=A1,B'=B1,C'=C0) that the model considers impossible violate I(A',B',C')=False.

b_rows_sample.anchor: 93.17 — Experiment 8 ... Crash creates Approved=True but ApprovalRecord=False. Expected: recovery must repair or reject the state. Result: PASS
b_rows_sample.statement: Experiment 8: a crash-created state with Approved=True but ApprovalRecord=False must be repaired or rejected by recovery; result PASS.

b_rows_sample.anchor: 93.18 — Write-ahead logging ... Log(T)→Apply(T)→Commit. After crash: Recover(Log).
b_rows_sample.statement: Describes write-ahead logging: Log(T)→Apply(T)→Commit, with crash recovery via Recover(Log).

b_rows_sample.anchor: 93.19 — Experiment 9 ... Committed operation appears in durable log but not yet in materialized state. Expected: recovery can replay the operation. Result: PASS
b_rows_sample.statement: Experiment 9: a logged-but-not-materialized committed operation can be replayed on recovery; result PASS.

group_evidence.why_grouped: explicit agent-stated uncertainty: 'reliability-fault-tolerance-recovery-model' POSSIBLY relates to 'concurrency-idempotency-replay-model' (batch B0024). Note: Step 93: models failure/recovery within the same mathematical framework (recovery is itself a governed transition). Covers transaction-boundary vs real-world side effects, outbox pattern, durability, write-ahead logging/event sourcing with event validation before append, checkpointing, idempotent retry and exactly-once-as-semantic-effect, partial failure with never-infer-from-absence (three-valued), compensation vs rollback with compensation provenance, recovery-must-not-erase-history, failure as observation vs cause as inference, recovery confidence/freshness, reconciliation, monotonic recovery (no silent downgrade), RPO/RTO and multi-dimensional recovery assurance, failure-domain independence, and fault-injection/chaos testing. Closely related to concurrency-idempotency-replay-model.

a_rows_sample.anchor: K1={a0,a_scan[id]} via o1; K2={a0,a_vendor[id]} via o2 ... A structural = : Pi is inside id -> different ids -> different sets: VACUOUS. B semantic == : equal IF Pi is discarded -- but that CHOICE is Decision 3, OPEN: SUBSTANTIVE *but see E2*. C observational ~ : equal under cardinality-only observation: SUBSTANTIVE relative to declared set. D provenance =_lam : explicitly compares Pi -> unequal by construction: VACUOUS.
a_rows_sample.statement: Re-runs the D285-5 action/result witness against all four corpus-named equality relations rather than the three previously tested, finding it vacuous under structural equality (as before), conditionally substantive under semantic equality only if a specific, currently-undecided discard-of-provenance choice is made, undefined-as-stated under observational equality pending a fixed observation set, and newly found VACUOUS under provenance-sensitive equality -- meaning two of the four relations make the property vacuous, one is conditional on an open decision, and one is undefined without further specification.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Corpus (246) defines FOUR relations: structural, semantic, observational, provenance-sensitive. 'history' equality is NOT among them. The chain 'history ⊊ structural ⊊ semantic' appears ONLY in verification-lane artifacts... => the HIERARCHY is a verification-lane construct (DERIVED), not CORPUS. ... structural ⊊ semantic WITNESSED. D ⊆ semantic BY DEFINITION. observational is NOT comparable without fixing the permitted-observation set.
a_rows_sample.statement: Corrects the previously-assumed three-level 'history subset structural subset semantic' equality hierarchy (used without verification in S2078's RQ mandate) by showing it is not actually a corpus-defined relation at all, only a verification-lane construct; the corpus's own four relations instead give a witnessed strict structural-subset-semantic inclusion, a by-definition provenance-subset-semantic inclusion, and an observational relation that is simply not comparable to the others without first fixing a specific observation set.

a_rows_sample.anchor: CORPUS — Step 246 defines, at state level: A K1=K2 structural (byte/structurally identical); B K1≡K2 semantic (encode the same knowledge semantics); C K1≈K2 observational (every permitted observation produces the same result); D K1≅_λK2 provenance-sensitive (content and relevant provenance equivalent) — 'These are not interchangeable.' CORPUS — Step 264.15 additionally defines semantic equality at value level: v1≡_D v2, with 3m ≢_str 300cm but 3m≡_D 300cm.
a_rows_sample.statement: Records the exact corpus citations (Step 246 for the four state-level equality relations, Step 264.15 for a parallel value-level semantic equivalence with a worked unit-conversion example distinguishing structural from semantic equality at the value level) grounding the corrected equality analysis.

a_rows_sample.anchor: structural=>semantic? True (witness holds). semantic=>structural? False => the inclusion is STRICT. provenance=>semantic? True (D is defined AS semantic+Pi). => structural⊊semantic WITNESSED. D⊆semantic BY DEFINITION. => observational is NOT comparable without fixing the permitted-observation set. The corpus hierarchy is a partial order over four relations, not the three-element chain previously cited.
a_rows_sample.statement: Executes the three testable inclusion implications among the corpus's four equality relations, finding structural is strictly contained in semantic (witnessed) and provenance-sensitive is contained in semantic (by definition), while observational equality cannot even be compared to the others without first fixing a specific permitted-observation set -- concluding the equality space forms a PARTIAL ORDER over four relations, correcting the earlier assumption of a single strict three-element total-order chain.

a_rows_sample.anchor: **The investigation has converged on two genuinely irreducible formal gaps:** 1. `Qualify` has no executable/formal body — `G1` ... 2. Three corpus equality relations lack decision procedures — also `G1`
a_rows_sample.statement: Identifies two genuinely irreducible formal gaps (both graded G1): (1) Qualify has no executable/formal body, remaining the blocker for making πK computable — Sanjaya recovers the missing referent/observation layer (W,Ω,O) but does not solve Qualify; (2) three corpus equality relations (≡ semantic, ≈ observational, ≅_λ provenance-sensitive) lack decision procedures — equality is not missing as a concept but is under-specified as an executable formalism, and the research should not invent another equality relation to make D285-5 work.

a_rows_sample.anchor: **The next logical research target is therefore not another Sanskrit hypothesis. It is the formalization of the corpus equality relations and `Qualify`, with the two kept strictly separate.**
a_rows_sample.statement: States the overall verdict and next research target: the three gap-update artifacts show real progress (moving from 'are we missing concepts?' to 'which recovered concepts are formally specified enough to support executable claims?'); the next target is not another Sanskrit hypothesis but formalizing the corpus equality relations and Qualify, kept strictly separate — this is where the investigation can either make πK computable or rigorously demonstrate why it cannot.

a_rows_sample.anchor: | Area | Current verdict |
a_rows_sample.statement: Freezes a 15-row status table as the current evidence state: W/Omega referent layer recovered/promoted; Observation closed as discovery gap; Sanjaya corpus-native six-valued structure; Jnana mapping corrected (Jnana~delta, not Knowledge); Knowledge primitive deliberately absent/corroborated; Kshetra/Kshetrajna ratified as genuine contribution; Karma/Phala corroborated but weakened to quotient-relative; Vairagya/outcome-independence independently supported; Sarathi/guidance-authority boundary independently implemented; K_atma destroyed; Theta_total rejected (does not type-check); Equality graded G1 (under-specified, not absent); =_semantic in D285-5 confirmed a methodological defect; history⊊structural⊊semantic is a verification-lane construct not corpus fact; Qualify still G1 and still the πK blocker.

a_rows_sample.anchor: **"What does each already-ratified equality relation mean operationally, and under what conditions can it be decided?"** That is exactly analogous to `Qualify`: the vocabulary exists, but the executable/formal body is missing.
a_rows_sample.statement: Reframes the equality research question away from 'what other equality should KnowledgeOS invent' toward 'what does each already-ratified equality relation mean operationally, and under what conditions can it be decided' — explicitly drawing the analogy to Qualify, where the vocabulary exists but the executable/formal body is missing.

a_rows_sample.anchor: `≈` is a **family** of relations indexed by an observation set, not one relation. ... `≈_𝒬` for a declared query set `𝒬`; and `𝒬` must be declared per bounded context
a_rows_sample.statement: Target 2 (≈ observational equality) is partially derivable: its form is derivable directly from its own definition — it is a family of relations ≈_𝒬 indexed by a declared observation/query set 𝒬, not a single relation — but the set 𝒬 itself is NORMATIVE and must be declared per bounded context (since K_A(Reality)≠K_B(Reality) is a corpus principle), and parameterisation (by Ω, role, access level, or purpose — all four appear in the Sanjaya principles) is left open. The permitted-observation set is undeclared per corpus Step 261 §261.23, which states the observation set 'is not fully closed.'

a_rows_sample.anchor: | **structural** | 🔴 **FALSE** | ... | **semantic** | ✅ **TRUE** | only after unpacking `Assertion` ... | **observational** | 🔴 **FALSE** | answerable in `(𝒜,ℛ)`: `member`, `contradicts`, `supersede`, `lineage`. **Not answerable: `replay`, `policy-eval`, `authorize`**
a_rows_sample.statement: Runs the three equality tests against the (A,R)=πK(K_t) claim: structural equality FALSE (πK's image is {Entity,Observation,Proposition,Relation,State}, target is {Assertion,Relation}, and Assertion is not a ratified primitive); semantic equality TRUE, but only after unpacking Assertion into {Proposition,Entity,Observation}+{id,c,t,Π} modulo the declared drop; observational equality FALSE — (A,R) can answer member/contradicts/supersede/lineage queries but not replay/policy-eval/authorize.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Under the verification lane's own identity rule `id = H(P, e, c, t, Π)`, **`Π` is inside the hash.** So `o₁` and `o₂` produce assertions with *different ids*, hence **structurally different states**, and the antecedent `δ(K,o₁) = δ(K,o₂)` is **false** — the property never fires. **It fires only under semantic equality**
a_rows_sample.statement: Shows the property is equality-relative: under structural equality (id=H(P,e,c,t,Π), which includes provenance Π) o1 and o2 produce different ids, so the antecedent is false and the property never fires — vacuously true and useless under structural equality, required and load-bearing under semantic equality, and required under observational equality.

a_rows_sample.anchor: **1** | ⚠️ **`history ⊊ structural ⊊ semantic` is NOT a corpus hierarchy.** Measured: it occurs only in verification-lane artifacts. ... *"these are not interchangeable."* **`history` is not among them.** My citation is withdrawn
a_rows_sample.statement: Amendment 1: withdraws a citation that had claimed 'history ⊊ structural ⊊ semantic' as a corpus hierarchy — measurement shows this occurs only in verification-lane artifacts, while the corpus (location 246) defines exactly four non-interchangeable relations (structural =, semantic ≡, observational ≈, provenance-sensitive ≅_λ), and 'history' is not among them.

a_rows_sample.anchor: $$ \boxed{ Invariant(P) \text{ is relation-relative where }P\text{ compares objects} } $$ For example, a transformation can preserve semantic state ... while changing ... structural
a_rows_sample.statement: Argues that any invariant comparing objects is relation-relative among the four equality relations (=, ≡, ≈, ≅_λ): a transformation can preserve semantic state (K_t ≡ K_{t+1}) while changing structurally (K_t ≠_structural K_{t+1}) because metadata/representation changed, and provenance-sensitive equality may distinguish states that semantic equality identifies.

a_rows_sample.anchor: under **structural equality**, the relevant antecedent can be false; under **semantic equality**, the witness becomes substantive, but only after choosing what semantics preserve; under **observational equality**, the result depends on the permitted observation set; under **provenance-sensitive equality**, the same witness can cease to establish non-injectivity. So **"equality" is not one mathematical operation in this programme.**
a_rows_sample.statement: Summarizes the D285-5 witness's behavior across all four equality relations as evidence that equality cannot be hand-waved: structural equality makes the antecedent false; semantic equality makes the witness substantive only after choosing what semantics preserve; observational equality's result depends on the permitted observation set; provenance-sensitive equality can make the same witness cease to establish non-injectivity — concluding 'equality' is not one mathematical operation in this programme but a family whose members must each be operationally decided.

a_rows_sample.anchor: if we encounter something of the form $$ K_1 \equiv K_2 \Rightarrow P(K_1)=P(K_2) $$ we cannot call that a final invariant until the semantics of `≡` are fixed. ... any invariant relying upon observational equality must carry that parameter. And provenance-sensitive invariants ... must remain conditional until "relevant provenance" is formally specified.
a_rows_sample.statement: Requires that any candidate invariant using an unresolved equality relation be marked explicitly conditional: a semantic-equality-based invariant is not final until ≡'s semantics are fixed; an observational-equality-based invariant must carry its query/observation-set parameter Q explicitly; a provenance-sensitive invariant must remain conditional until 'relevant provenance' is formally specified.

a_rows_sample.anchor: $$ \Sigma_1\approx_X\Sigma_2 \iff \pi_X(\Sigma_1)=\pi_X(\Sigma_2) $$ is a very useful reduction, but it does **not** choose which `X` KnowledgeOS should adopt. b_rows_sample.anchor: Until now we have used Zero intuitively as 'the gap between where we are and where we need to be.' We now need to make that statement mathematically precise. The decisive test is: Can Zero(K,G,EC) be computed from the KnowledgeState? If yes, Zero becomes a genuine computational primitive of Knowledg
b_rows_sample.statement: Frames Step 25D's decisive test: can Zero(K,G,EC) be computed from the KnowledgeState, making Zero a genuine computational primitive rather than an AI metaphor.

b_rows_sample.anchor: A conventional system might define Delta=Target-Current. That is insufficient for KnowledgeOS. ... Nexus version known/3.69 known, Rollback verified/unknown, Firewall permitted/conflicting, Architecture approval/missing. There are four fundamentally different situations. Therefore Zero != simple sub
b_rows_sample.statement: Corrects the naive Delta=Target-Current model of Zero using a four-requirement worked example (known/unknown/conflicting/missing), establishing Zero≠simple subtraction — it must compare requirements against epistemic state.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Let the goal be G. The goal induces a set of required knowledge conditions: R_G={r_1,r_2,...,r_n}. For Nexus migration ... r_1=CurrentVersionKnown ... r_7=GovernanceApprovalObtained. This is crucial: Zero cannot be computed from the goal alone. We need the Epistemic Contract that tells us what must
b_rows_sample.statement: Defines the Knowledge Requirement set R_G induced by a goal G (worked with seven Nexus-migration requirements r1-r7), establishing that Zero cannot be computed from the goal alone and requires an Epistemic Contract.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Define EC_G=(R_G,Gamma_G) where R_G = required conditions; Gamma_G = rules determining sufficiency. So EC_G = what must be established + how sufficiency is judged. This gives Zero a formal input.
b_rows_sample.statement: Defines the Epistemic Contract EC_G=(R_G,Γ_G) — required conditions plus sufficiency rules — as Zero's formal input.

b_rows_sample.anchor: For each requirement r_i, we evaluate its status against K_t. Define Sat(K_t,r_i). Initially I propose the following state set: S={Satisfied, PartiallySatisfied, Unknown, Insufficient, Conflicted, Stale, Invalid, Prohibited, NotApplicable}. This is already much richer than Boolean logic.
b_rows_sample.statement: Defines a nine-value requirement-satisfaction status set (Satisfied, PartiallySatisfied, Unknown, Insufficient, Conflicted, Stale, Invalid, Prohibited, NotApplicable), explicitly richer than Boolean logic.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Suppose Sat(K,r)=False. That could mean: we know it is false; we don't know; evidence conflicts; evidence is stale; evidence was invalidated; governance prohibits the action. These are operationally very different. Therefore Sat != Boolean.
b_rows_sample.statement: Argues Sat≠Boolean: a bare False collapses six operationally distinct situations (known-false, unknown, conflicting, stale, invalidated, prohibited) into one indistinguishable value.

b_rows_sample.anchor: We can define Z_i=Status(K_t,r_i,EC_G). Then Zero(K_t,G,EC_G)={(r_i,Z_i) | r_i in R_G}. This gives us a Zero vector. For example Z(K)=[Satisfied,Satisfied,Unknown,Insufficient,Conflicted,Satisfied,Missing]. Now Zero is computationally representable.
b_rows_sample.statement: Defines Zero(K_t,G,EC_G)={(r_i,Z_i)} as a computationally representable 'Zero vector' of per-requirement statuses.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Case A: No evidence exists: Evidence(r)=empty. Status: Unknown. Case B: Governance requires approval, and no approval exists. That is Missing. These are different. So I recommend Missing as a separate status where the requirement itself is an expected governed artifact/action.
b_rows_sample.statement: Distinguishes Unknown (no evidence exists at all) from Missing (an expected governed artifact/action, such as an approval, that does not exist) as two different status values.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Suppose current KnowledgeState contains A_1: NexusVersion=3.69, A_2: RepositoryCount=43, but nothing about rollback. Then Status(r_1)=Satisfied but Status(r_3)=Unknown. If Architecture Board approval is explicitly required and has not been issued: Status(r_7)=Missing. Therefore Zero(K)={r_3:Unknown,
b_rows_sample.statement: Worked Nexus example computing a concrete Zero(K)={r3:Unknown, r7:Missing} from partial knowledge state evidence.

b_rows_sample.anchor: We can therefore define Zero(K,G,EC)=R_G \ Satisfied(K,R_G) but this is only a shorthand. The real result must retain why each requirement is not satisfied. So Zero={Requirement, Status, Evidence, Reason, Dependencies}.
b_rows_sample.statement: Corrects a shorthand set-difference definition of Zero (R_G minus satisfied requirements) into the fuller structured form Zero={Requirement,Status,Evidence,Reason,Dependencies}, retaining why each requirement is unsatisfied.

b_rows_sample.anchor: A Zero item should look conceptually like: Requirement: RollbackVerified; Status: Unknown; SupportingEvidence: none; BlockingReason: no successful restore test; RequiredAction: perform restore test; DecisionCriticality: high. This is already implementable.
b_rows_sample.statement: Gives a concrete implementable structured-Zero-item template with six fields (Requirement, Status, SupportingEvidence, BlockingReason, RequiredAction, DecisionCriticality).

b_rows_sample.anchor: Suppose E_1 supports RollbackVerified=True. Is that enough? Not necessarily. The epistemic contract may require 2 independent tests. Or 1 test witnessed by a designated authority. Or Probability(success)>=0.99. Therefore Satisfied = ContractSpecific.
b_rows_sample.statement: Establishes that satisfaction of a requirement is ContractSpecific — the same supporting evidence may or may not count as satisfied depending on the epistemic contract's own sufficiency rule (independent-test count, witness authority, or probability threshold).

b_rows_sample.anchor: We therefore need Satisfied(K,r,EC) which may invoke the appropriate reasoning model. For example Satisfied(K,r,EC)=RuleEngine(K,r,EC) or =StatisticalCriterion(K,r,EC) or =HumanAuthorization(K,r). This is another reason Zero must not contain one universal inference mechanism.
b_rows_sample.statement: Defines the satisfaction predicate Satisfied(K,r,EC) as potentially delegating to RuleEngine, StatisticalCriterion, or HumanAuthorization — reinforcing that Zero must not embed one universal inference mechanism.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Zero should not calculate everything itself. Instead: Zero -> RequirementEvaluation -> AppropriateReasoningModel. ... Zero aggregates the results.
b_rows_sample.statement: Establishes Zero as an orchestrator that dispatches requirement evaluation to the appropriate reasoning model (Rules/Statistics/Authority) and aggregates results, rather than being an inference engine itself.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Operational Zero: Z_W=Distance(W_t,W*) where W* is the target world state. Epistemic Zero: Z_K=Distance(K_t,K*_EC) where K*_EC is the knowledge required by the epistemic contract. These are fundamentally different.
b_rows_sample.statement: Formally splits Operational Zero Z_W=Distance(W_t,W*) from Epistemic Zero Z_K=Distance(K_t,K*_EC), reaffirming the two are fundamentally different quantities.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Target: Nexus Pro running in target environment. Current world: Nexus OSS 3.69 running. Operational gap: Z_W>0. But suppose Target architecture known, Current version known, Backup status unknown, Firewall status unknown, Approval missing. Then Z_K>0. Even if an engineer knows exactly how to perform
b_rows_sample.statement: Worked example showing Z_K (epistemic gap) can independently block execution even when the operational how-to is fully known, illustrating Z_W and Z_K as genuinely separate blocking gaps.

b_rows_sample.anchor: I recommend Zero=(Z_world, Z_knowledge, Z_governance, Z_decision) at the conceptual level. Z_world: What differs in reality? Z_knowledge: What required facts are unknown/uncertain? Z_governance: What required approvals/rules are missing? Z_decision: What prevents a defensible decision? This is much
b_rows_sample.statement: Decomposes Zero into four conceptual dimensions (Z_world, Z_knowledge, Z_governance, Z_decision), each answering a distinct question, stronger than a single scalar distance.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Suppose Z_knowledge=5 and Z_governance=1. Can we say Zero=6? No. The six missing items are not necessarily comparable. One missing governance approval could be more blocking than five low-priority informational gaps. Therefore Zero is primarily a structured object, not a scalar.
b_rows_sample.statement: Counterexample against summing dimension counts into a scalar Zero=6: a single governance gap can outweigh five informational gaps in blocking severity, so Zero must remain primarily a structured object, not a scalar.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Once the structured Zero exists, we may calculate: GapCount. Or CriticalGapCount. Or WeightedGapScore. Or ContractCoverage. For example Coverage(K) = satisfied required conditions / total required conditions. But these are projections of Zero, not Zero itself.
b_rows_sample.statement: Defines four derivable scalar projections of the structured Zero object (GapCount, CriticalGapCount, WeightedGapScore, ContractCoverage), explicitly distinguished as projections, not Zero itself.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Each requirement can have Criticality(r) such as {Critical,High,Medium,Low}. But again, we should be careful with arbitrary scores. A critical requirement might be RollbackVerified. If Status=Unknown, then migration could be blocked regardless of all other results. This gives us BlockingCondition.
b_rows_sample.statement: Introduces per-requirement Criticality with a caution against arbitrary scoring, deriving the concept of a BlockingCondition — a single unresolved critical requirement that blocks regardless of all other results.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Evidence != Interpretation ... Kernel != AI Brain.
a_rows_sample.statement: Complete 17-invariant catalog: Evidence!=Interpretation, Evidence!=Justification, Justification!=Conclusion, Assertion!=Truth, Authority!=Truth, Confidence!=Truth, Unknown!=False, Conflict!=Rejection, Supersession!=Deletion, Representation!=Identity, Semantic similarity!=Identity, Reasoning!=Validation, Model!=Reality, Association!=Causation, Knowledge Product!=Knowledge, KnowledgeOS!=Reasoning Engine, Kernel!=AI Brain.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Closed-world assumption: If it isn't recorded, assume false. ... Open-world assumption: If it isn't recorded, truth status remains unknown. For epistemic engineering, many knowledge questions require the second. This is particularly important for AI agents. ... Unknown ≠ False.
a_rows_sample.statement: KnowledgeOS should explicitly distinguish closed-world assumption ('if it isn't recorded, assume false') from open-world assumption ('if it isn't recorded, truth status remains unknown'), arguing epistemic-engineering questions -- especially for AI agents -- generally require the open-world reading; restates the invariant Unknown != False and warns 'no evidence found' must not be conflated with 'evidence does not exist.'

a_rows_sample.anchor: Unknown must be a legitimate state. Not: Unknown = False. Not: Unknown = Null either. Because null is a technical representation, while UNKNOWN is semantic. ... L = {True,False,Unknown}. For some verification operations we may need: {Pass,Fail,Inconclusive}. These are related but not identical. Verification = INCONCLUSIVE does not necessarily imply Claim = UNKNOWN.
a_rows_sample.statement: Unknown must be a legitimate semantic state, distinct from both False (Unknown!=False) and from a technical Null (Unknown!=Null, since null is a technical representation while UNKNOWN is semantic). Proposes a three-valued epistemic logic L={True,False,Unknown} alongside a related but non-identical verification-outcome logic {Pass,Fail,Inconclusive}; a Verification=INCONCLUSIVE result does not necessarily imply Claim=UNKNOWN since the verification method itself may simply lack sufficient evidence. Restates the statistical-discipline rule: 'no evidence' implies 'insufficient evidence', not 'negative conclusion', unless a closed-world rule is explicitly declared for the domain.

a_rows_sample.anchor: I1: Observation ≠ Interpretation I2: Evidence ≠ Knowledge I3: Determination ≠ Decision I4: Decision ≠ Authorization I5: Authorization ≠ Execution I6: Unknown ≠ False I7: Provenance ≠ Lineage I8: Memory ≠ Historical Continuity I9: Recommendation ≠ Decision I10: Evidence must be traceable to its source. These should become candidates for the KnowledgeOS semantic constitution.
a_rows_sample.statement: Consolidates a candidate ten-invariant set (I1-I10: Observation!=Interpretation, Evidence!=Knowledge, Determination!=Decision, Decision!=Authorization, Authorization!=Execution, Unknown!=False, Provenance!=Lineage, Memory!=Historical Continuity, Recommendation!=Decision, Evidence must be traceable to its source), explicitly proposed as candidates for a future 'KnowledgeOS semantic constitution' -- not yet ratified.

a_rows_sample.anchor: ObservedResult = ∅. But: TrueResult ∈ {Success,Failure}. Therefore: ObservedResult missing ⇏ TrueResult = Failure. This is exactly the same epistemic principle we established earlier: Unknown ≠ False. ... It would be dangerous to automatically record: Failure.
a_rows_sample.statement: Reframes an unconfirmed execution result (e.g. a command issued but connection lost before confirmation, ExecutionStatus=UNKNOWN) as a missing-data statistical problem: ObservedResult=empty does not imply TrueResult=Failure, restating Unknown!=False in the execution-outcome context and warning it would be dangerous to auto-record Failure for a merely unconfirmed result.

b_rows_sample.anchor: one aggregate with two parts, or two aggregates sharing an identity? ... I-4 is itself a spanning invariant — a negative one.
b_rows_sample.statement: Facing evidence that no positive invariant spans the lifecycle and authority parts of the record (an honest finding that argues for splitting), the proposal nonetheless keeps one root because I-4 (they must never merge) is a negative spanning invariant needing a single holder that can see both parts, and the write boundary is one file.

b_rows_sample.anchor: (D) invariant violation — NO ... (D), and the defect is in the proposal's I-5 row, not in the invariant, the mechanism, or the model.
b_rows_sample.statement: C-3's classification is independently derived (before reading the refinement's own reasoning) as (D): the observed non-Governance recorder on a HANDOFF transition is not an invariant violation, missing enforcement, or a missing conceptual distinction, but simply a table cell in the proposal that measured I-5 (an authority-part invariant) against a lifecycle-part transition, which I-4 itself forbids conflating.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Verdict: (D) — a mis-scoped invariant statement. ... D.1 — The observation and the invariant live in different parts of the aggregate.
b_rows_sample.statement: Independent classification (derived from evidence E-1..E-8 before considering any candidate) concludes (D): the observed `architecture`-recorded HANDOFF is not a violation, missing enforcement, or missing distinction, but a case of measuring an authority-part invariant (I-5) against a lifecycle-part transition, which I-4 itself forbids; both instances were also the mechanism's required actor (DP-3), and a HANDOFF confers no ownership regardless.

b_rows_sample.anchor: OQ-12 | Should invariants carry an explicit enforcement class — refused · overwritten · not-consulted · writer obligation? ... OQ-13 | Is authorizationLinkage a modelling element or a query convenience?
b_rows_sample.statement: Two new open questions are raised without proposed solutions: whether invariants should carry an explicit enforcement class distinguishing refused/overwritten/not-consulted/writer-obligation (OQ-12), and whether the identity query's authorizationLinkage is a modelling element or mere query convenience (OQ-13).

b_rows_sample.anchor: 'Consistency is determined by invariant ownership, not by event-driven communication.' ... EKS: No event bus. Yet: 11/11 workflow invariants → single identifiable owner → executable tests ... SUPPORTED: non-distributed systems / UNKNOWN: distributed KnowledgeOS
b_rows_sample.statement: DeepSeek tests and finds current consistency is achieved through invariant ownership, not event-driven integration: EKS has no event bus yet 11/11 workflow invariants have a single identifiable owner with executable tests; PKS has no event architecture yet governance invariants define ownership; AIP has no event-driven architecture yet BC-7 mechanically owns orchestration invariants. Explicitly does NOT over-generalize: classified SUPPORTED for non-distributed systems, UNKNOWN for a distributed KnowledgeOS.

b_rows_sample.anchor: C-17 Authority enforcement ... E — MISSING ... C-18 Temporal reconstruction of authority ... 2/218 transitions carry any date field ... E — MISSING ... C-19 Cross-process coordination / provenance attestation ... E — MISSING ... C-20 Delegation ... OBSERVED BEHAVIOUR — SEMANTIC INTERPRETATION UNKNOWN
b_rows_sample.statement: Of 22 catalogued EKS capabilities (C-01..C-22, mostly class A implemented), four stand out as gaps: C-17 Authority enforcement is class E (MISSING, no implementation evidence at all); C-18 Temporal reconstruction of authority is class E (only 2/218 transitions carry any date field); C-19 Cross-process coordination/provenance attestation is class E; C-20 Delegation is explicitly re-classified (an archaeology-hardening correction) as 'OBSERVED BEHAVIOUR — SEMANTIC INTERPRETATION UNKNOWN' rather than implemented-but-implicit, since 0/126 grants carry any delegation, validity, expiry, ownership, or session-linkage field.

b_rows_sample.anchor: 11 of 11 workflow-record invariants have a single, identifiable owner and an executable test. Every invariant outside the workflow record either has no owner or has an advisory-only owner.
b_rows_sample.statement: Invariant-ownership table finding: all 11 workflow-record invariants (Inv A-J, G-2/G-3, R8) have a single identifiable code owner and an executable test (mostly class A); by contrast grant-identity uniqueness, temporal ordering of authority, and process/actor authenticity have NO owner at all (class E), while corpus reference integrity, identifier uniqueness, document schema conformance, and placement correctness have only advisory-only owners (class C) -- 'every invariant outside the workflow record either has no owner or has an advisory-only owner.'

b_rows_sample.anchor: I-4 registry != authority, never merged; I-10 the record outranks prose
b_rows_sample.statement: AIP's own invariant: I-4 registry != authority, never merged; I-10 the record outranks prose. The authority record is the per-work-item transition+grant log; the session registry is separate and is not authority.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Mechanically enforced invariants ... all contract-pinned by tests
b_rows_sample.statement: Mechanically enforced (contract-pinned by tests): I-1 exactly one mutation owner; I-2 HANDOFF and human START (neither alone yields ACTIVE); I-3 STOPPED is sticky (only CONTINUATION exits); G-1 closure is a governance act (COMPLETE refuses non-governance writers); G-2 Authority State has exactly one writer (grant writer rule R5a/R5b).

b_rows_sample.anchor: Declared-only invariants (NOT mechanically enforced)
b_rows_sample.statement: Declared but not mechanically enforced: R-34 producer != acceptor; INV-ATTR-2 separation is declared, not attestable; AIP-11 supersede-never-in-place; AIP-14 Product Primacy; I-4 registry != authority, never merged; I-10 the record outranks prose.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Every invariant BC-7 (the workflow engine) owns is mechanically enforced; almost every invariant outside BC-7 is declared only
b_rows_sample.statement: Headline structural finding -- the invariant asymmetry: assurance is strong where it is executable (BC-7) and weak where it is prose (outside BC-7). 'The platform mechanically protects orchestration, and protects knowledge/verification/communication only by declaration.' Stated as the single most important structural property of AIP's current architecture.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Headline structural findings
b_rows_sample.statement: Seven headline findings: (1) AIP is a registry-first, session-based engineering operating platform, not a product domain; (2) the implemented core is the workflow/authority engine plus guard surfaces, with knowledge/review components deferred/not built and verification under construction; (3) the invariant asymmetry is the load-bearing structural property; (4) the authority record lives in an ignored runtime directory (the durability inversion), decided-but-not-executed; (5) the D1/D2 decision state is contradictory across the corpus, surfaced not reconciled; (6) four unowned capabilities form one control loop with C-10/C-14 existence UNDECIDED; (7) AIP self-records four capability failures (EKS-01..04) -- the platform observing its own uneven assurance.

b_rows_sample.anchor: IMPLEMENTED != VERIFIED != ADOPTED != AUTHORIZED (§38) -- this review establishes readiness for the fourth-to-third transition and leaves ADOPTED and AUTHORIZED untouched.
b_rows_sample.statement: Confirms and applies the four-state lifecycle model (IMPLEMENTED, VERIFIED, ADOPTED, AUTHORIZED as four distinct, non-collapsible states, §38) as load-bearing governance vocabulary: a PASS review moves work from VERIFIED toward being ready for the ADOPTED decision, but does not itself adopt or authorize, and the adoption decision belongs solely to the PO/ARB.

b_rows_sample.anchor: IMPLEMENTED the capability, document and contract test were produced (this slice) / VERIFIED independent verification of the produced work (PENDING) / ADOPTED governance-path adoption decision by the PO/ARB (PENDING) / AUTHORIZED authorized for future use as the operating model (PENDING)
b_rows_sample.statement: Originates the four-state completion model (IMPLEMENTED / VERIFIED / ADOPTED / AUTHORIZED) as a required, never-collapsed distinction in the implementing session's completion report -- the same model later confirmed and applied throughout S0374-S0382.

b_rows_sample.statement: Register census, Established rows: INV-001 Evidence != Authority; INV-002 Observation != Decision; INV-003 Assessment != Authority; INV-004 Projection != Source -- all registered at UM-24 settle, validation state Established, lineage HPA synthesis INV-001..004, validated cross-system tier-1/2.

Transformation family: INV-002 STRONG (ESTABLISHED) -> KERNEL(established), SURVIVES (law 4); INV-004 STRONG (C-7, ESTABLISHED) -> KERNEL(established), SURVIVES (law 5); INV-KOS-001 STRONG (SS31 score-collapse) -> KERNEL, SURVIVES (law 2, the general anti-collapse law whose named instances are INV-001..004 + Expression!=Meaning + Observation!=Inference); H-KOS-NonInterference-001 MODERATE (ruled OVERLAPPING with INV-KOS-001) -> KERNEL, SURVIVES/CONSOLIDATE into law 2; INV-KOS-Revisability-001 STRONG (C-2/C-5) -> KERNEL, SURVIVES (law 11, folding in the Temporal family); INV-KOS-Decision-001 STRONG (the decision-collapse target) -> KERNEL, SURVIVES (law 4).
